bio:
Artist Hyo-jin park has been working with the sea for a long time. The infinite rhythm and change of the image of the wave, as well as the loneliness and energy of recovery hidden within it, have been a deep inspiration to the artist.

In her early work, she looked at the sea as a realistic landscape, but she did not stop at simply describing the facts. She tried to convey the emotions and thoughts she felt through the movement of the waves, and read the tension, relaxation, and hope for life contained within them.

The Beautiful World series was born in this extension.

The early works of this series paradoxically tell the story of beauty blooming in adversity. It was an attempt to hide pain and sighs and instead sublimate them into a clearer and more tranquil screen. By revealing the depth of emotion but expressing it in a restrained manner, simplifying the image of the wave, and utilizing the blank space, she wanted to create a space where the viewer could project their own story.

She began to think about more abstract and implicit language, moving away from the realistic and concrete wave landscapes she had previously used, and this was a turning point for me as well. With this series, I wanted to explore the possibility that beauty is not simply a visible landscape, but can still shine despite the wounds and adversities of human beings.

My gaze is still on the waves, but I wanted to tell a deeper and more universal story beyond them.
I am moving from the familiar image of the sea to paintings that can contain more emotion, lingering feelings, and the complexity of life.

bio:
With a foundation in industrial design, Mee Ha has navigated diverse creative realms—from product and brand identity to UX design. Along the way, she recognized that design thinking—fluid, intuitive problem-solving—is the essence of all creation. The more she explored this concept, the more she saw parallels between human thought and liquid: ever-shifting, adaptive, and boundless. Every object—headphones, watches, shoes, and clothing—originates from thoughts that morph, evolve, and solidify over time.

This realization inspired Ha to visualize the fluidity of ideas through art. Intrigued by the nature of liquid materials, she began reimagining the objects that define modern life in liquid form. Her series, Liquid Things, explores urban existence by merging advanced digital technology with handcrafted techniques, capturing fragments of contemporary culture through a dynamic, shifting lens.

Each piece in Liquid Things carries layered meaning. An object’s purpose changes depending on who perceives it, where, and when—while others reflect the cultural shifts of an evolving world. To highlight these nuances, Ha embeds invisible messages into her works using materials that mimic the transparency and movement of water. These hidden inscriptions emerge only under light, creating a subtle interplay of humor, social commentary, and deeper reflection. She describes them as “water graffiti”—whispered messages that transform ordinary objects into storytelling artifacts, revealing their ever-changing connection to the world.
This realization led her to explore the fluidity of ideas through her art. Fascinated by the nature of liquid materials, she began reimagining objects integral to modern life as liquids. Her works, Liquid Things, focuses on objects that represent urban living, combining advanced digital technology with handcrafted techniques to portray fragments of contemporary life.

Each object in Liquid Things carries multiple layers of meaning. While the same item may serve different purposes for different people, others reflect shifting cultural contexts over time. To capture these nuances, Ha incorporates transparent phrases into her work, using materials reminiscent of water. Initially invisible, the messages reveal themselves under light, offering viewers a subtle interplay of humor, cultural commentary, and deeper reflections. She refers to these inscriptions as “delicate graffiti,” embedding messages that elevate each object’s narrative and connection to the world.

bio:
Hyeok Eon Kweon
Korean Painter
Born in 2001, Lives and works in South Korea.

Hyeok Eon Kweon is a Korean artist whose works primarily feature hummingbirds as a central motif. He began painting hummingbirds during a period of severe lethargy and anxiety, using art as a way to overcome his inner struggles. For Kweon, the hummingbird is a guiding presence, leading him forward on his artistic and personal journey. His works reflect resilience, hope, and the search for light amidst darkness.

Recently, Kweon held a solo exhibition at KV Gallery in Busan Citizens Park. He also participated in the 4th “100 Artists 100 Works” exhibition at Beeum Gallery in Insa-dong and Ajit Museum of Art. His artistic achievements have been recognized by the Daegu Fine Arts Association, where he was awarded a Special Selection in the Western Painting category at the 42nd Daegu Art Competition.

bio:
Ryu HoiMin(류회민) -

The reality is that the deep, dark ink is being overshadowed by the overwhelming momentum of brilliant colors, losing its vitality. Eyes accustomed to pink tones can no longer accept the seemingly dim and lifeless black of the ink. The desire for color is boundless; countless vibrant hues—either blends of primary colors or even more finely subdivided shades—constantly pour out from pigment factories. To those intoxicated by color, the black ink that represents the achromatic may be intolerable.
​Nevertheless, my ink grows thicker and thicker. No matter how much water-based ink is layered on a flat surface, it never seems to possess a physical texture. Yet, in anticipation of a transformation, I endlessly repeat the process of accumulating ink (Jeokmuk). In doing so, I eventually move beyond scorched ink (Chomuk) and reach a realm of oily brilliance.
​Since I work primarily with ink, I must focus on the movement and flow of the ink tones to maximize the effect of illusion using only black. To overcome the limitations of representing objects in a single tone, I am compelled to devote my efforts to the diverse variations and profound depth of the ink's shade.

bio:
Kwon Yongbin explores the quiet tension between light, time, and the human presence that lingers within ordinary landscapes.
Working across seascapes, water studies, and minimal still-life compositions, he approaches photography like a form of listening—observing how light moves, gathers, dissolves, or leaves a trace on the surface of the world.

His recent series investigate the rhythmic structure of water and the subtle emotional spaces found in the everyday. Influenced by music, especially the atmospheric phrasing of jazz, his work shifts between realism and abstraction, revealing moments that feel both familiar and distant.

Across all subjects—sea, people, water, or objects—his practice remains consistent:
to capture the silent intervals where perception slows down and the world briefly aligns with memory, sound, and light.

Based in Seoul, he continues to build a body of work that bridges fine-art photography, contemporary abstraction, and personal narrative.

bio:
I am an artist who breathes life into the moon.

My journey as an artist began during my time as a truck driver. On lonely nights on the road, I found profound comfort in the moon, and I intentionally sought it out in the night sky. My art stems from the longing I felt on nights when the moon was hidden from view.

In my work, I always paint a full, complete moon. This is my way of expressing the comfort and presence I desire, not only for myself but for everyone who looks to the night sky for solace. Through my oil pastel creations, I aim to share the gentle warmth and unwavering comfort that the moon has always offered me, hoping my art becomes a sweet breath of moonlight for you.

bio:
The series  began with a longing for metaphorical, abstract, and yet concrete works. 
Many of my paintings are made up of small dots. Small dots symbolize stars. To me, stars are life itself, transcending time and space. They are longing and connected to hope. The countless stars that always shine unchangingly above our sky come to me as longing and memories that meet as the boundaries of time and space blur, and as comfort that they still exist somewhere.
When I think of the countless stars that seem to pour down from the sky, I feel a miracle. Living as a human being on a planet in our galaxy within the infinite universe and countless galaxies must be a magical miracle that touches an unfathomable fantasy... So when I think of the stars in that endless universe, I think of the existences in countless times and spaces, and I also think that maybe someone I miss exists somewhere. So when I look at the stars, the boundaries of time and space disappear, and my longing turns into possibility, and that comes to me as comfort.
I am painting each star with a prayer for life and peace.

bio:
Yim Choon Lee’s painting “Black Hole” elicits visions of movement, eruptive, confusing, and dizzying.  These feelings of movement gravitate the viewer into a wondrous cosmos of twisting layers and colors, drawing feelings of awe and questions of how its creation is possible.

Yim has invented a new technique incorporating sculpture and painting called “Tearing Art”.  This technique offers a three-dimensional experience, creating a desire to reach out and touch the various textures within.
Born in Goseong, Korea in 1965, Yim inherited three-generations of Korean traditional bamboo and paper art.  

At age 5, he began to learn these skills from his father.  Together, they traveled throughout the mountains in Korea to collect the bamboo for his father’s bamboo art. The bamboo art has a major impact on Yim’s paintings.  

When Yim was 9 years old, he went to a bamboo mountainside with his father.  Waiting through a sudden rainstorm, Yim watched the swaying of the bamboo leaves in the wind.  With the background of the mountains, Yim saw a wave of colors that rocked through the entire mountainside.  This illusion was the most beautiful scenery he had ever seen.  He wanted to transform this phenomenon to a canvas.  

Ever since, Yim has experimented with various materials and techniques to create his three-dimensional paintings on canvas.  In the development of his art work, Yim started with Korean traditional paper and bamboo art, then experimented in paintings with soil and sand, and further used Korean traditional paper with light.  Later he applied western oil to Korean traditional paper which created a unique style and texture. From there, he expanded his art horizon to include sculpture, installation art, and performance art.


Yim has invented tearing art.
Since 2010, Yim has experimented with a totally new technique: tearing the canvas. After removing the canvas, Yim places Korean traditional paper on top of the frame and paints in layers.  He then paints both side of the canvas and replaces it upon the frame.  Next, he cuts or tears the surface of the canvas and twists or folds it to reveal the back side’s paint. With this method, the colors of the three surfaces blend dynamically and create a unique visual effect. 

The three surfaces of painting represent the past (traditional paper surface), present (back of canvas linen), and future (front of canvas linen).  In tearing art, one painting glues together the past, present and future in three dimensions.

Yim has invented Sola halo technique.
Solar halo technique is to use acrylic and mother-of-pearl on canvas.
Solar halo technique is an original technique of modern art developed by Yimchoonlee and it is completely different from the existing method of using mother-of-pearl.
The natural light and color of the mother-of-pearl cannot be expressed well on the camera.
In reality, it creates a fantastic mood that looks like a jewel in it.

bio:
I'm an American artist currently working out of my studio in South Korea where I've been for the past 20 years.
I primarily work in oil abstraction but also watercolor landscape painting.
My works are inspired by memories--mental images of landscapes that are recalled, reimagined and transfigured as paintings.  These views are constructed not based on the order they appear in visual reality, but rather after filtering through thought and memory.  The works attempt to depict visual recall of a scene(s) in fragmented, abridged, and altered perceptions reconstituted in one image.
Memories are often inaccurate and biased according to our beliefs, expectations and hopes, as well as our life experiences.  How we process visual input is also affected by these personal characteristics.  Ask two people to describe the exact same place they have both just visited and you will receive two differing descriptions regarding the details.  What we recall, how we recall, and the hierarchy of importance are highly individualized.
These works are relatively devoid of any concrete representation and are intended to hint at rather than specify for the viewer.  Functioning as suggestion for thought or feeling, it is up to the viewer to come to their personal conclusions regarding meaning or paths to meaning.
To generate meaning from a non-representational image demands a longer look, a reflection and projection of free thought and associations.  They will likely mean something different for each viewer as it is only natural to bring to an image all personal experience and memory.  However, it is the process of looking and analyzing your own wonderings that is in itself the message.  Look, and look again.

bio:
My work begins at the point where familiar spaces and landscapes meet inner emotion. Through vivid color and fluid spatial composition, I explore how emotion, memory, imagination, and nature intertwine. Everyday places are transformed into psychological landscapes shaped by personal experience and reflection, while spaces that move between interior and exterior expand into sensory environments.

Using acrylic paint for its quick-drying qualities and rich pigmentation, I seek a balance between spontaneity and deliberate structure. Within each brushstroke, I aim to capture subtle emotional shifts, gradually dissolving the boundaries between reality and imagination. This process leads to what I describe as a “garden within the heart”—a space where calm, solace, and quiet contemplation reside.

I currently present my work actively in both domestic and international art fairs and group exhibitions. Grounded in traditional painting practices while engaging with contemporary conceptual inquiry, my work opens a dialogue between the viewer and the image. By exploring personal inner landscapes, I seek to reveal shared human emotions and consider the restorative potential of art in contemporary life.

By covering discarded materials with natural fibers, the sculptures highlight environmental pollution and biodiversity loss, delivering a message of hope for what is disappearing.

bio:
Munsan Kim Young-sik, who runs Joseonyo under Haneuljae in Gwaneum-ri, Mungyeong-eum, Gyeongsangbuk-do, is the only 8th generation owner in Korea.  He is the eldest grandson of the oldest pottery making family.

Kim Yeong-sik has been in the family for generations since his 8th great-grandfather, Kim Chwi-jeong, first started spinning on a pottery wheel 240 years ago.
They own and preserve the kiln that has been firing white porcelain for 170 years.

This kiln is designated as Gyeongsangbuk-do Folk Cultural Heritage No. 135. It is a Mangdaengi kiln built with clay that has been shaped like a mortar and dried, 
and the fact that it has not collapsed even over a long period of time shows the family's history.

His works are made using pottery techniques passed down from generation to generation, using clay and glaze from the Mungyeong region, and are natural and simple.
And you can see that there is sincere generosity and lack of greed.

 The Mungyeong white porcelain living pottery stands out for its artistic quality by depicting simple figures. 
Above all, what he devoted all his energy to for a long time was making tea utensils for tea lovers using traditional pottery gibabs that had been passed down for generations.

Different types of tea bowls for matcha and tea sets for chariots are produced using various clays and glazes.

His works are made using pottery techniques passed down from generation to generation, using clay and glaze from the Mungyeong region, and are natural and simple.
And you can see that there is sincere generosity and lack of greed.

bio: Born in Seoul in 1982, she debuted as an artist in 2008. Her early works were influenced by animation and featured autobiographical characters expressing themes of loss and isolation, often visualized through physical holes in the canvas as symbolic escape routes. She has since explored the deconstruction of pictorial surfaces and, since 2019, has expanded her visual language through digital animation. Since 2023, her Borderline series has explored a new visual language where painterly depth and digital immateriality intersect. Her current practice spans short animations and media art, reflecting a continued interest in cross-genre experimentation

bio:
Artist Jui Lee, who is always concerned about what is defined by others, embodies unrealistic images of reality on the screen, making us think about what is real or what is fake. In terms of materials and techniques, various coloring tools such as oil painting, acrylic, stone powder, oil pastel, and charcoal are used to create a colorful feeling.

In terms of content, even cognitive tension is sophisticatedly resolved by adding geometric patterns to realistically depicted scenes to make them appear unfamiliar. Therefore, artist Lee Jui's work allows us to imagine the story hidden behind visible objects, allows us to see what we see differently, and allows us to feel the dual charm of actively speaking to the audience while seeming to hide what we want to say.

Reason for recommendation
Could it be that we are so busy with what we have been given that we are bored with the boredom of everyday life? What you need to escape this boredom is a new perspective on everyday life that is unfamiliar to you, and a fresh stimulus that allows you to see it that way. Author Jui’s work is enough to provide fresh stimulation. The repetitive geometric patterns within the work create a sense of rhythm, and you can experience the expansion of a two-dimensional plane into a three-dimensional space. In addition, restrained colors bring out special emotions, and the relativity evoked by the contrast between black and white makes rigid thinking flexible. This weighty and original work will make your daily life special.

bio:
I am Wondeuk Cho(1991-birth), an artist based in South Korea.

I create works that depict and interpret scenes from landscapes I have personally observed while living in Korea.

My work aims to offer a new interpretation of spaces that are both uniquely Korean and deeply personal, as I strive to create a complete and introspective realm of my own.

Below is a text that organizes my thoughts as an artist. Thank you.

——————————————

"Mountains embody an unwavering solidity amidst infinite changes, a paradoxical nature that fascinates me about ordinary, everyday natural spaces. They steadfastly maintain their position and form, shaped over centuries. However, within their depths lie countless entities constantly born, dying, moving, and transforming, creating myriad narratives.

My goal is to observe landscapes authentically and create tranquil, liberating spaces. Though my process is repetitive and labor-intensive, it allows for moments of self-cultivation, filtering through 'self' to craft new natural environments. This pursuit seeks to establish a space where freedom and unrestricted existence are paramount."

bio:
I like blue. That draws a lot of blue sky and sea. In blue dreams, hopes, future, determination, enthusiasm and acclaim. Through my paintings I hope you think for a moment to dream.

Memory gradually fades, gets erased, and gets fragmented as time passes. Scents that had felt nothing special at first and landscapes that slid by can stay in memory. However, after time passes, memory splits a bit by bit and goes into an attic called forgetfulness and gets piled up. And it gets all mixed up. 

The same goes for the memories from trips. Beautiful landscapes, tasty foods, or even great music slowly go inside darkness and fade. They can be found only at the moment we are confronted with some elements of memories that we can connect or when we intentionally try to pass through the memory tunnel inside our brain since we miss the previous trip. 

Traveling is a little fantasy in life. We can live an unrealistic life that we have dreamed of when we stop for a while doing things that we do for our daily life. We can get up late, not hurry, eat delicious foods, or drink coffee at an open-air café, watching people. Or, we can choose not to do anything. The time of our everyday life stops while we travel. We can even live a life as if we are not ourselves but some others. However, traveling always has an end. Perhaps, the reason traveling is a beautiful fantasy is because there is an end. 

How about love, then? Doesn’t it resemble traveling to a degree? We live, always dreaming of a love that is breathtakingly beautiful just like we live, dreaming of a trip. Like we live others’ lives during taking trips, we change as if we are not ourselves when we fall in love, become so generous and passionate to our sweethearts, and hope for our future. However, even a fantasy as a heartfelt love comes to an end as time goes. This is painful and beautiful as well since we always have limited time. 

Finished trips and fantasies about love turn into longing and get stored. We remember the summer night we spent in the Seine, Paris, and miss our painful first loves we had in our early twenties.    

I work on this subject of “memory” because I want to stop the moments for a while before the tunnel of my memories all shut down. But I can only remember some impressive parts and most parts are getting filled with margins; but there is someone that I miss, and there is love, longing, loneliness, happiness, and sorrow in the margins. 

I hope my paintings get stored in your memories and also hope that you hold on to your fading memories.

bio:
Kim Chong kyo is a Korean fine art photographer who explores the profound stillness and subtle beauty of nature through conceptual minimalism. His work captures fleeting moments of silence — a lotus in quiet bloom, a pine forest shrouded in mist, or an egret descending through still air. Rooted in the traditional aesthetics of Korean calmness and spiritual reflection, Chong kyo’s images are meditative visual poems.
He has been recognized in multiple national photography contests and continues to develop series that reflect both personal faith and universal tranquility.

The artworks inspiration from the simple joys of everyday life - picnics, travel, and time spent with family. These familiar scenes are painted with the colors of childhood happiness, innocence, and nostalgic memories.

At the heart of each piece is the owl character 'Ungsoon', who embodies the wide range of emotions and joys found in our daily lives. Ungsoon's family go on adventures together, enjoy picnics, support one another, and share warmth and laughter.

Through the sweet and gentle world of Ungsoon I hope to spark delightful imagination in children, while evoking the warmth, love, and childlike wonder that adults carry in their hearts.

bio:
My practice is dedicated to the exploration of diversity, individuality, and liberation through art. My work is a celebration of the unique beauty inherent in every person, challenging societal norms and facilitating a deep dive into the essence of one's true self.
I seek to break free from restrictive ideologies and prejudices, pursuing an artistic expression that fosters unconditional acceptance and profound respect for diversity. Each piece is conceived as a visual sanctuary where the individual is stripped of external expectations and encouraged to embrace their most authentic state.
Furthermore, my art serves as a gentle reminder not to overlook the exquisite light that resides within us all. In a world often clouded by external pressures and complexities, it is easy to forget our innate radiance. Through my creations, I aspire to nudge the viewer toward self-discovery, cherishing the noble light that still guides us, and embracing the intrinsic, unblemished beauty of the human spirit.

Furthermore, my art reminds us not to forget the beautiful light within each of us. In a world often clouded by external pressures, it's easy to overlook our innate and exquisite radiance. Through my creations, I aspire to gently nudge us to rediscover and cherish the noble light that still resides within us, guiding us on a journey of self-discovery and embracing our intrinsic beauty.

My work ranges from realistic depictions of apples to interpretations using the fundamental elements of art—dot, line, and plane—exploring both two-dimensional and three-dimensional forms across various genres. The handwritten, doodle-like lettering is reinterpreted as lines and shapes, becoming part of the composition. In this series, my signature style is vividly expressed through bold use of color and dynamic compositions. Each piece features meticulously rendered animals, such as cats and dogs, nestled within fashionable handbags. This creates a playful contrast between the softness of the animals and the structured elegance of the accessories.

bio:
I began drawing at an early age, spending my childhood in a small village at my grandparents' house. Surrounded by the beauty of nature—fields, rivers, and animals—I was constantly inspired by the life around me. I had my own little studio with a drawing table, pencils, and watercolors, where I would capture scenes of trees, forests, animals, people, and various objects. I even created illustrated stories that brought my imagination to life.

For me, every element in nature has its own unique spirit, whether it’s an animal, plant, stone, or water. I aim to infuse each piece I create with a sense of life, inviting viewers to feel the soul of what I paint.

bio:
Artist Lee Kang-yoon is a dedicated artist who has built his own style of painting through repeated experiments in formulation. Natural communication and fundamental vitality have been expressed through unique colors, compositions, and unique molding techniques. I met an artist who contained memories of his days and childhood and listened to the heart-warming art world.



capture pure childhood memories on the canvas

Artist Lee Kang-yoon's canvas is peaceful. It gives a rest in the warmth of the primary color. The humorous and pure expressions of the half-naked children are impressive, and the sight of running around with cows, dogs, and birds in nature and forming a beautiful harmony reminds me of the Garden of Eden full of happiness. As a child, the artist, who grew up on an ocher farm and interacted with nature, captures pure and fresh emotions and memories on the canvas.

"I'm over 70 years old, and it's hard to find a happy time in my life. Still, my childhood was the happiest time when I played naked, so I drew it after I was 50 years old."

This artist's brush touch is concise and light in both lines and sides. The painting is implicit, and the primary colors of yellow and green are mainly used as the background color to add a warm feeling.



Focus on image simplification

This artist presents an implicit image. Talk to the audience with a more symbolic image.

"The more I know about painting, the more difficult it is. When I was young, I tried to work on non-ideal images with only style and blood, but as time went by, I began to see paintings little by little by little. Should I say that my perspective on painting has deepened a little over the years?"

Artist Lee always studied his work in a new direction and sought change, finding himself focusing on simplification work as he grew older over the years.

"Even if it's a little difficult and difficult to work on, I want to draw brightly." To that end, I try to think positively about everything and express it honestly. Also, as the whole work brightens up, I feel a change myself."


I will walk the path of art with a good heart

Artist Lee built the depth of art by studying for 24 years from the late Song Hye-soo, a representative writer in Busan. Starting with his early non-ideal vision and beginning to sketch, he is always trying to have a good influence on the world as a writer, bearing in mind his teacher's teachings that "people should be first and work on paintings."

"There are often paintings that neither the artist nor the viewer can recognize each other. This is not only because there is no firm subjectivity of the artist, but also because the work is weak. When we listen to good music, or when we look at a great painting, it has a good influence on everyone regardless of what kind of thing it is. Therefore, a good picture can be created only when the artists' skills are raised to a certain level."

As such, artist Lee said that the artistic level of not only the artist but also the person who appreciates and treats the painting is important, stressing that the diversity of the work should be recognized through in-depth appreciation. Artist Lee then said, "If you're drawing, you shouldn't let go of your brush. I've never put down a brush even in the past when it was difficult. It may be hard now, but the world where art is the mainstream is bound to come. "I hope everyone who wants to make the world happy with their brushes will do well and stay healthy," he said, not forgetting his advice for junior writers.

Artist Lee Kang-yoon is preparing for a retrospective exhibition to commemorate next year's landscape. Prior to the exhibition, he expressed his determination to focus on simple work and said he would strongly convey the message of a happy life in his life.

bio:
My paintings focus on the surface as a field of interaction, not a finished image. They explore the balance between intentional gestures and unpredictable material responses.
Surface conditions — absorption, texture, and flow — interact with paint density to create a visual field that never fully resolves.
The work captures moments of tension between control and unpredictability, and inviting close observation, to reveal a subtle interplay of color and texture that changes with light and distance.

In the ‘Accumulation’ series, layers are built through the repeated acts of layering and overturning paint. As oil and water-based materials repel each other, they produce unpredictable densities. Consequently, the surface becomes a physical record of time rather than a single, static decision.
In the ‘Surface’ series, absorption and resistance coexist. Raw fabric draws in the paint while coated areas block it, creating a palpable tension between openness and closure. Rather than a uniform plane, the painting transforms into a field of shifting conditions.
I am interested in structures that do not resolve. Instead of stability, my work holds a sustained state of imbalance - a quiet negotiation between intention and matter.
Through the accidental marks of layering, I invite the viewer into a space of constant becoming.

bio:
Park Lia (real name is Valeriia Kapitulska) is a Ukrainian artist based in Seoul, South Korea.
She works primarily with acrylic on canvas.
Her practice focuses on landscapes and quiet everyday scenes, exploring the relationship between nature, light, and stillness. Through simplified forms and a restrained color palette, she reflects moments of pause and inner calm.
Park Lia’s work is influenced by her experience of living between cultures and observing ordinary environments with close attention. Her paintings emphasize atmosphere rather than narrative, inviting slow contemplation.

She creates original artworks and limited series intended for residential and public interiors.

bio:
I am a painter currently living and working in Seoul, South Korea. 
I constantly explore and reinterpret the natural elements that symbolize the flowing time, such as waves, wind, and plants, in an abstract manner, filling the canvas with memories of past experiences in nature. Alternatively, I depict the process of visualizing everyday landscapes into abstract expressions, bringing the memories of nature into actual or artificially created architectural spaces to evoke individual inner memories. 

I aim to evoke memories and imagination of nature in viewers through brushstrokes that float, reflecting the rhythm and colors experienced in natural landscapes from a distant perspective. By observing landscapes from a distant vantage point, I want to invoke a sense of connection to nature and evoke the viewers' own memories and visualizations of nature.

bio:
Artist Seung-Yeon Moon graduated with TOP honors from Ecole Nationale Supérieure des Beaux-Arts in Toulouse, France. Every moment now instantly becomes the past. Moon wants to capture the meaning of the time that unconsciously passes us by.

  She suggests a break for everyone to have a thought and to appreciate the very moment through the eyes of her object and innocent animals that seemingly just jump out from fairy tales. Her works come with several distinctive personalities. Moon depicts huge eyes; she wants people to reflect themselves through the big eyes and to fall into the time of what they recall from those pupils. Animals in her paintings could be the best friend, family or favorite pet; there is no hierarchy in the relationship and they stay forever together unlike reality. The teacups appearing in her every art pieces are totally subjective according to each spectator; they may contain hot, cold, full, empty or even somewhere in the middle. Everyone interprets different facial expressions from the same look. She allows the public to have their own imagination of how they truly feel. The backgrounds of the artworks change over time because it reflects unique experiences or dramatic changes in the artist’s own life. The fundamental belief of the artist, however, stays the same. She believes that real love is to take care of who you care

bio: I am active in Korea. I am expressing a universal human form.While living in the present era, The question that began with my own curiosities, "What is the most important thing as a human being in this age?" created the process of finding various spaces inside of me. If you broaden your vision, you will find that there is a desire to constantly study and develop yourself, and you will concentrate on the inside of the existence of "me" or "us." From the observer's point of view, I tried to face the inner world with a cool mind, and based on this, I repeated meditation and imagination as a way to derive something deep inside. My work is not on the outside of human, but on the inside. And this is the work of elicit out the candor. The more I repeated the work and studied the method, that is the more I felt that it was close to raw, rough and free. In addition, in order to think about whether this is universal, we sought a lot of advice and captured opinions, which showed that the inner parts of human beings were somewhat similar. Most of them showed weakness and were able to collect the fact that they had some sort of packaging to hide their weaknesses. Therefore, I realized the keyword of Normal Human and necessary the inner space for ordinary people to stabilize. And through this, I felt that another space was needed to connect various inner spaces. As I was deeply fascinated by the inner side, I thought about creating a Hub Space that voluntarily created the inner side of the center that close to perfection. But it can't be designated by others, so I'm going to ask myself questions through work and give you a message to create a voluntary Hub Space through it. Hub space is a kind of control space. I suggest that by showing the inside of ordinary people and the HubSpace that they make spontaneously, we must ask ourselves back the natural and unnatural phenomena that are derived from humans and develop them. When asked what would be the process of creating Hub Space, I convey that it is only one's own will and thoughts about it. These things will pile up to create a complete HubSpace, and they are essential for living in this day and age. Because the most important thing for these Normal Humans in this day and age is their own core. Absolutely, humans cannot live an ordinary life, and there is no definition of ordinary daily life and life. Knowing yourself is a weapon, not knowing yourself is a weakness. By presenting these two things, I want you to finally meet yourself completely, acknowledge your own lowness, and ask yourself how you can develop yourself.

bio:
Choi Haeng-sook is referred to as a painter of ‘’一揮揮之'.
’一揮揮之' refers to expressing strong vitality with a single brushstroke.
She captures intense vitality with just a single brushstroke.

Choi Haeng-sook's major works are largely divided into the 'Vitality' series and the 'Arirang' series.
‘Vitality’ is a black work in a monochrome style.
And 'Arirang' is Korean traditional music that is registered as a UNESCO cultural heritage.
 
Both series are painted with a single brush stroke.
“Painting with just one brush at a time” is a method of drawing on the canvas with just one stroke using a wide brush.
 
'Arirang's vitality' refers to the curves and dance moves of the top hat that can be seen in Pungmulnori, a traditional Korean dance, the rhythmic melody of the hem of a traditional Korean skirt, and the 'vitality' contained in the rhythm of 'Arirang' music. do.
The 'Vitality' series is the result of a unique method created by overlapping such images.
As a result, the strong will to live extends beyond the canvas.

bio:
Tak Jion is a South Korean ceramic artist whose work is rooted in the philosophy of “Hee-Haeng” — coexistence, companionship, and a movement toward hope. To visualize this, she developed “Moorisae,” stylized bird forms that she has refined over years of exploration. Each bird is composed of 5 to 20 hand-carved lines, capturing the essence of flight and simplicity. When gathered as a flock, these birds create unified rhythms and emotional resonance, embodying the collective spirit of Hee-Haeng.

Her inlaid ceramic slabs are entirely hand-carved and framed, using the traditional Korean sanggam technique — carving patterns into clay, filling them with colored slip, and refining the surface after drying. These works are not mere decorations, but conceptual spaces: records of movement, traces of emotion, and a quiet pursuit of connection. Through the Moorisae, Tak Jion builds a visual metaphor for moving together — in life, in hope, and in harmony.

bio:
Using oil on canvas or panels, Molly presents stories in a lyrical and fairy tale bizarre atmosphere, mainly featuring unfamiliar forest landscapes with boys and girls who have not yet grown up.
In a post-community society where criticism, prejudice, and irresistible huge discourses abound, modern people unconsciously admit their wrongdoings and end up losing their ego by throwing themselves into the mysterious world like a boy lost in the forest.

-The artist projects modern people accustomed to anxiety and loneliness on a boy who is lost in the forest. In particular, she believes that the fear and anxiety of modern people living in the pandemic era have resulted in the ephemeral nature of another life, like the medieval vanitas painting, and that the symbols of loss, wounds, and fears have grown to become wild and huge forests within each of them.

-Molly Kim graduated from Ewha Womans University with a major in Clothing and Textiles and has been working as a full-time artist since 2014 after working in the fashion industry for more than 15 years. She had 10 solo exhibitions, including a booth exhibition at Seoul Art Museum and various selected group exhibitions. She has received numerous awards, including the 2019 ASYAAF Hidden Artist selection.

I am an artist who expresses my ideas through figurative art in the form of digital painting.

bio:
Melody Park (b. 1987) lives and works in Seoul, South Korea. She holds a BA in Fine Art from Kingston University, and an MLitt (Drawing pathway), also in Fine Art, from the Glasgow School of Art. 

She is an artist who is quicker with her hands than with her head. She is not beholden to plans or preconceived notions about the finished article. She prefers to let the work unfold of its own accord. There is a spontaneity and serendipity about her work process. Such a process tends to produce more abstract pieces. She has an intrinsic visual and spatial curiosity, and interests in the relationships between colour, shape, objects, and the body. She is inspired by her daily life and she believes that art is the experimental research arm of our studies into the everyday.

bio:
I draw people’s thoughts in my own way.
Every person thinks.
And the colors, feelings and features of thoughts are very diverse.

I started to have interest in ‘thought’ during the conversation with people. Sharing thought brings new idea and sometimes it develops philosophy and ideology. 

Those thoughts are very similar to nature.
Various trees, flowers, leaves, and living things harmonize and meet to form a single mass. They are connected and form a flow. And it becomes a forest like a community.
Both thought and nature have the organic flow, various shapes and colors. They are connected to each other.

I focused on this natural curved flow and colors and expressed in the work with my own spirited shapes and colors. Sometimes my trees look odd and even bizarre, because trees in my painting are not only the appearance of nature, but also the images of various thoughts and memories.
They are trees of thoughts and birth from the seeds of thoughts. And there is no limit in expression. 

Also, when starting a work, firstly I think about main colors that can represent the meaning of each work's thoughts. Some colors give you vitality, while others calm your mind. I used colors to convey my intention and bring the connection with viewers. 
Books are also major subject in my painting, because books are a collection of thoughts.

I express books through various situations or my imaginations. 
In addition, you can see the flying fish in every work of mine. Flying fish is my symbol.

The fish got feathers and wings, got out of the water, and it became Flying fish. Flying fish travels freely all over the world and spreads people’s thoughts from here to there. Sometimes Flying fish is the transportation of travelers, carrying books (the collected body of thought) and guides wanderers.

I hope that the viewer will receive warm energy or a moment of comfort and healing with my color in artworks.

bio:
artist / drawing based on pen / live in Seoul, Korea /

Description of work - Sometimes when I read a novel, I would read a author's note. Many of them talked about the motivation which makes writers who they are. When I read those calm and looking back of their own lives notes, I can see that there is desire that prove who they are and it is melted into the strong drive of life. And in the hidden side of those note, there's a memory of threat derived from unproven self. Sometimes It's overwhelming to feel the power of anxiety and insecurity between relationship. Those anxiety and insecurity make people doubt themselves and choose the wrong way to avoid threat. Like a famous Friedrich Nietzsche quote "And when you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss also gazes into you.", An obsession with an incompleteness passes throughout the life and shake the ego to its very foundation.
  
 'Parade' series is a process to make a caricature of an anxiety and 'Infected' series is based on a minute observation. My self-observation is concluded this sentence 'Look at the anxiety around you clearly'. And it is most important rule which i want to get not to feel insecure and self-conscious and to protect myself. To see oneself in an objective way prevents a reproduction and to stretch the meaning of anxiety. 
 
 'Infected' series is basically an extension of self-observation. In these series, a psychoneurotic disease is not a disease which is caused by virus infection but caused by increasing anxiety. And I observe the state and depict the state of an infection in this series. I want to gaze ailing self through observation and expression and to grasp the truth of anxiety. 
 
 Spread of negative memories and obsession with an incompleteness are the most serious problems for me to be fulfilled to be appropriated. My works start from sleep which is a kind of lack but in the base of it there are deep anxiety and dissatisfaction throughout whole life. I want to find my own way by observing enormous insecurity which makes me keep go on.

bio:
My drawings explore time. Time, not only gives a life to all living things, but also transforms space into place for them. My interest is to record this kind of ‘time’.

I begin with a dot(a line), and repeat dots(lines). A dot(A line), drawn with dark graphite or red paint, marks a ‘moment’ on paper. By repeating dots(lines), the moments grow into an ‘occasion’. The occasion, accumulation of moments, is finally reborn as a metaphorical entity. 

The impulse for tracing, recording, and marking moments is inescapable. So I draw.

bio: Through my work, I try to express the realm of everyday life in a sensuous form rather than a logical description. I think that emotional exchange can take place based on each audience's anxiety and inner feelings and can be displaced into the realm of communication. In it, a horizontal relationship between the past and the present, inside and outside, private and public, culture and another culture, and the time of me and the other is connected, forming a horizontal relationship of numerous stories stacked on top of each other. Just as elements that are hybrid rather than pure, elements that are eclectic rather than clean, and elements that are ambiguous rather than clear, are more attractive than those of perfection. The cracks contained in this process are dismantled in a simple and direct way to lead to a new mass (sculpture).

bio:
I lived a normal life while working at a job that started in my 20s, but I started painting by chance 4 years ago. There are close to 40 paintings. Inspired by listening to Ladygaga's song 'Always Remember Us This Way', the pop star series draws pictures to remember their most splendid moments.
 
At every moment, through all the noise, the tone of Ladygaga's song approaching me is indescribably attractive. Ladygaga, who has a sparkling aura, drew with the initials of 'LADYGAGA' in English the intense shouts of fans and the message of passionate support and cheering. As the artist said, the objects of the painting make the heart beat, and the artist expresses their language through painting. You can see how great they are through the pictures and record their shining moments. I express the inspiration I feel while listening to music with flowers, stars and letters, and draws people in various forms. So, I created my own way of drawing a picture called 'Shape Art'. Shape art is a method of drawing people with shapes, shapes, letters, and figures.

Pop singer 'Adele' painting hopes that her life will be as happy as a rosy life, and when I work with roses, I use shape art for the first time using a rose flower frame of various shapes devised by the artist myelf. Since then, I started painting people with flowers, stars, and letters, using various works such as letters, figures, lines, and planes. Each person has a different feeling, so drawing people with poker cards or filling the screen with only dark lines to draw life.

The pop stars appearing in my paintings deeply influence the invisible part of the my life. I love music receive comfort through songs, feel youthful, and dream. I use the pop singers who inspire me as my muse and draw them to be remembered as splendid moments. Perhaps because the painting contains the artist's thoughts that the painting seems to be talking when looking at the painting, when looking at the my painting, You can hear the singing voice. When you see my painting.

Hundreds of roses symbolizing eternal youth, 'BTS', the seven paintings expressed in colors that match the aura of each individual, 'Adele', the first painting painted with roses, her voice that breaks through every noise at every moment, 'LADYGAGA' ‘Ladygaga’ drawn with the initials, ‘Black Pink’ drawn in the shape of a star that looks like a goddess amidst countless stars, ‘Katy Perry’ drawn in the shape of a stick as if the stars are dripping in the night sky with the aurora unfolding, ‘ 'Eminem' drawn with the initials of 'EMINEM', 'Britney Spears' drawn with waving waves and furrows with lines, 'Rihanna' expressed with cherry blossoms fluttering in the wind in the night sky, Gangster rapper '50 Cent' drawn in a rectangle by analogy with a boxing ring. The Chaesobat depicts their most splendid moments.

bio:
I paint my art work with theme of 俱生我執(구생아집,Gu Saeng A Jip) which means there is substantial ego that is unchangeable. In the other words, my art work tells about obsession of my innate ego; the obstinacy. When we hear obstinacy, it gives us negative feelings and it contains negative meanings but ironically I love my obstinacy. It is the belief that there is immortal and indestructible ego which preside the objects in our body and soul. I tell this story through my painting by creating new world which I created through the obstinacy. This world is fresh and it is not ordinary nor smooth at all. In my work art, Self-attachments and personal stories, depression, Aggressiveness, selfish, honesty are connoted.
In modern days, I don’t try to hide my obstinacy. Due to this mind set my subjects of art work are striking existence in anywhere. As this world is filling with selfish of aggressive people who tries(try) to lower my self-esteem, I am more obsessed with my ego to survive in this world which is in dilemmas of depression. I am intoxicated with depression in order to be who I am, therefore I speak and act as I think and feel through my art work .
My motto is to create art works with message which is “Don’t make a mistake with locking yourself up by following trends and fake lip-service in this splendid world, disgorge your obstinacy like child without any bias.”

bio:
Roger Shepherd is a New Zealander based in Korea. He works full-time as an individual freelancer, specializing in Korean Mountain Culture from North & South Korea. His main mediums are photography and photo-art book publishing, but is now branching into painting as his new medium of expression. 

“Covid-19 suddenly provided me with a hole to fill. So I decided to use the spare time to fulfil a promise to my high school art teacher that I would one day draw again.”

Roger is the first person to have explored the Baekdu-daegan (a 1400km mountain spine of the Korean peninsula) in North Korea over several visits and the first foreigner to have walked and documented the Baekdu-daegan in South Korea. He has held several photo exhibitions throughout South Korea, as well as in Pyongyang, Kyoto and New Zealand. His exhibitions and photo art books of the Baekdu-daegan symbolize Korea as one mountain and one people. 

“I am a supporter of self-determination for the Korean people. Through arts, I aim to create a paradigm for the peaceful coexistence of North and South Korea. I seek commonalities rather than differences." 

Roger also runs a hiking company called Hike Korea, which has helped him discover most corners of the Korean peninsula. For the past ten years, he has been guiding foreign visitors to South Korea on their mountain hikes here, including a backpacking adventure in North Korea. 

 “These paintings are my first pieces. I decided to start with the Baekdu-daegan mountains of North Korea as they are my normal photo-subject material. I know them. Plus, no one has ever painted some of these rare unvisited peaks before. One day in the future when all Koreans are free to travel over their land, they will want to go north and south and see these peaks and places in real life. I hope that is in my lifetime.  As my vision and skill for painting (hopefully) increases, I am not sure in which direction my paintings on Korea will go, but I suspect they will leave the hills and go into the town centres and start to provoke there.”

로저 셰퍼드는 남한과 북한의 산(山) 문화를 글과 이미지에 담는 화가요 사진가이자 저술가로서, 여러 번의 방문을 통해 북한 지역의 백두대간을 탐사한 최초의 인물이며 산행을 통해 백두대간을 사진과 저서와 미술작품들로 기록한 최초의 외국인이다. 그는 평양, 쿄토, 뉴질랜드를 포함, 코리아의 전역에서 남북한에 걸친 백두대간의 산들을 하나의 산, 하나의 민족으로 상징하여 보여주는 사진전을 여러 차례 열었다. 저는 한민족의 민족자결 원칙을 지지하며, 미술작품과 행동주의적 활동을 통해 남한과 북한의 평화공존을 위한 하나의 패러다임을 창조해내는 작업을 하고 있습니다. 저는 산과 미술과 문화를 한 무대 위에 올림으로써 거주하는 지역과는 상관없이 맥맥이 흐르고 있는 한민족의 동질성을 부각시키고자 합니다.

그림은 제가 어떤 기술도 없이, 고심해본 적도 없이 마구 덤벼든 일이 아닙니다. 어릴 적에 저는 언제나 그림 그리기를 즐겼는데 학교 선생님들도 그걸 알아보시더군요. 하지만 사춘기로 접어들면서 시작된 십대의 모험과 스포츠 활동이 그림을 계속 그리고자 하는 욕구를 눌러버렸습니다. 그래도 저는 고등학교의 미술 선생님들과는 잘 통했고, 열여섯 살 때 고등학교를 나와 자동차 도색공이 되자 선생님들은 최소한 제가 색채를 조화시키는 법은 배우게 될 거라고 밝게 격려해주셨습니다. 그들의 말은 틀리지 않았습니다. 쉴즈 선생님은 정색을 하며 저에게 언젠가는 다시 그림을 그려보라고 하셨습니다. 저는 그 말을 한 시도 잊지 않았습니다. 당시로서는 학교를 나와 힘든 도제생활을 한다는 게 그리 신나는 일은 아니어서 그 선생님의 말씀이 가슴 한구석에서 늘 빛이 되어주었던 것 같습니다. 그때부터 저는 언젠가는 다시 그림을 그리게 되리라는 직감을 품고 있었습니다. 하지만 그 전에 저에게는 다니며 경험해야 할 일들이 있었습니다.

bio: Korean Oriental & Contemporary Artist

Won Hee-su is Painter in Republic in Korea. She captures her emotions and thoughts comes from various factors surrounding her, such as nature, music, movies, and social issues, on canvas.

“My art alternates between the explosive expression of the senses and the delicate realization of emotions. I communicate with the canvas with strong and also emotional brush touch to embody the energy of aspiration that boils within me and the impulses deep within me on the surface. Painting is a deep and personal work process for me. I express my inner energy and various influences and inspirations from external stimuli to the world. In an endless world of imagination, I face infinite possibilities."

Playing in the imaginary world and the world of the senses, she expresses her inner senses and emotions with free colors and materials. Through the character Q in some pictures, she asks questions about life and creates her own answers through work.

bio:
When I was young, I sat by the river and looked at the twinkling waves of sunlight without knowing time was passing.
I used to look at the waves moving as if they were alive.
Looking at regular but non-regular waves makes you feel comfortable.
Water absorbs and projects everything and reflects the subject without revealing itself.

bio: Hello, I'm Mijin Jung, an artist based in Korea. I capture the warmth of everyday moments in my artwork, hoping to bring a sense of comfort and reflection through each piece.

I try to recreate the landscapes within my inner self, depicting them as new and utopian nature through simple lines and shapes
I pursue the beauty of simplicity that reveals the essence of landscapes, just as ancient cave paintings depicted everything with a single stroke. The simple and rough brushstrokes, yet rich texture create landscapes that are neither distorted nor exaggerated, giving a sense of comfort and familiarity.

Born into a traditional woodwork family, I was captivated by the color red from a young age, because the traditional woodwork made by multiple layers of lacquering on wood exhibits subtle and varied range of red color. Thus to me, it is the most Korean color connected to our traditions, and the main element in expressing the liveliness and warmth of our homeland

For a long time, I have been painting 'Sky and Land,' by symbolizing the sun, moon, stars, clouds, mountains, trees, etc. in one space. In the past, the landscape used to be my hometown, but recently it’s cosmic nature from my imagination

bio:
Using black ink, repeatedly fill in the white screen with dots and lines.
It is called black bait, but the color of ink is called brown in the East. "Hyun" is a profound word meaning black, black light, sky light, sky light, far away and profound. Just as black but fine red and blue, and the color of the night sky is not completely black, the color of ink is a complex color that is hard to define in a word. At first glance, the color of ink differs depending on the time of ink production and the wood used as a material, and the emotions felt by the surrounding environment, space, and light are similar to human emotions.

"When I first used ink ink many times, I started to get inspiration from Venice's Sea of the Night. In 2017, I felt a different emotion when I saw the sea that looked black on a small bridge in Venice. When I saw the sea at night in Venice, I felt uncomfortable but uncomfortable, like a vague and endless floor, if I had received positive emotions such as rest, sunny, bright, and exhilarating. Seeing the swaying of the black sea, I thought it was perfectly similar to the color of ink, and I would like to convey the feelings I felt at that time to visitors.

It's a dictionary definition of repeating the same thing.
It is an act of repeatedly putting ink with a brush, but the result of repeated ink is different every time. It is a repetition of behaviors with different results. It leaves its own country by repetition and creates another mark on it, creating a space of 'empty' weight. The more you repeat, the deeper the empty space becomes, and there is a place where emotions permeate every corner of the space. It is to create a space that exists and does not exist, as if we were looking at a virtual space in the mirror.

They work while comparing repetitive actions to human life. An incident that leaves a mark on a life resembling white paper, and each person's personality, characteristics, and personality appear and live their lives. Speak more narrowly, in comparison to each day. Many people think that life has no special meaning and that boring life repeats itself. But I think that day will come together and become the only person. While thinking about this, the work created by repetitive actions shows the same pattern and appearance at first glance. It's the same way, and if you look closely, it's a completely different result. Even in relationships between people, this kind of thinking creates a lot of conflict. The easy way of thinking that the emotions you feel and the way you think are similar because you look like yourself leads to misunderstanding of the relationship with others and causes small and big problems. It means that people should recognize that they are similar but distinctly different individuals and pay attention to them.

bio:
The artist's interests were always ordinary and quiet, and he had a habit of observing his surroundings. The observed landscape was ideally reinterpreted and led to a painting. 

Real places photographed in daily life and travel become the basis of the painting, and we study and express unique vivid and soft colors to capture the contrast between the bright flow of light and the shadows. 

The artist's work becomes an ideal space in harmony with vibrant objects, nature, and architectural spaces. I hope that viewers can take a clear break with this clear and warm ‘light and shadow’ and the expression of a wide space.

In addition, the artist communicates deeply with the subjects and tries to focus. As a result, my inner self communicates with them, and the product of that communication is captured in the picture. A typical example is the plumeria flower.

The white plumeria flowers in the work were seen by the artist while traveling in Vietnam. A fragrant rest under a plumeria tree during the trip has become an unforgettable experience, and fragrant flowers emerge as an ideal identity to emulate with a desire for healing and well-being.
(Flower language: ‘Lucky to have met you’ or ‘Blessed person’)

The artist believes that the world seen through the eyes of the heart will lead our lives to be enriched. It contains the desire to spend a leisurely day in a rewarding and busy life of hard work.

bio:
Born in South Korea
Live & work :  Berlin <-> South Korea 

Jazoo Yang is a Korean mixed media artist based in Berlin. She often distorts public spaces to profound ends. With a mixture of concept-focused art and an intriguing visual palette, she questions the relationship between ourselves and the spaces that we inhabit. Her more recent practice has focused on the transformation of housing in the city and the gentrification that is pushing local residents from their homes. The 'Materials Series' is an amalgamation of the diverse, the distant, and the disregarded. Formed of the lost fragments of urban life that she rescues before their inevitable disappearance – remnants of a building’s outer walls, scraps of wallpaper from an interior, the remains of antique tiles – these often silent, ignored objects are here transformed from the mundane, and framed to acknowledge the immensity of the intimate. 
 
Furthermore, while developing projects related to the issues of redevelopment, Yang keeps an interest in what the original senses of human beings might be like within the rapid changes of a city. The speed of city life runs much faster than that of the human body, thus enforcing its speed on the people living in that city. This situation, maybe even a violent one, may damage delicate aspects of the human senses. 
 
Yang is not only concerned with the material elements that make up our cities and about those living there, she also devotes herself to the details of natural systems, which unfold in urban space, yet remain invisible.

bio:
Elly Cho has exhibited around the world and holds numerous awards. Her art explores the intersection between nature, the environment and human behaviour, across various mediums including mixed media, video and performance art.

Cho’s approach to art making, is largely inspired by the relationship between nature, environment and the viewer’s perception to nature based on their personal history.
She approachs the subject matter of cultural landscapes in narrative form, and these narratives often relate to her own life experiences and memories. In her video work, She has used familiar landscapes that stimulate viewers to engage with an imaginative response.
Her recent research about color, nature and mental health brought new body of work that explores the relationship between ecology and human existence. By drawing on colors and movement of nature, aesthetic of being, and poetry in nature. She trys to mimic the movement of the species and then expanding the drawing to a more imaginary scene of poeticism. She feels that nature is a place where everyone feels to be part of and even if we are all apart from each other, being in nature, makes us together and connected.  Through her work, She seek to instill in the viewer a highly charged but nostalgic awareness of things long since past. She aim to experiment further, encouraging political engagement that allows both artwork and environment to jointly contribute to current artistic discourse. 

Cho’s awards include Sunny Art Prize in London, Award Winner of The Best Experimental Film, Best Silent Film, Best Dance Choreography Film, and Best Director at Cannes World Film Festival, Berlin Shorts, New York International Film Awards, ARFF Barcelona /Around International Film Festival, Oniros Film Awards, Best Actor& Director Awards New York among others. Her work has screened at film festivals such as 'AVIFF' Cannes Art Film Festival and Asia Film Art International Film Festival in Hong Kong and “Times Square Midnight Moment” in New York. Her residency participation includes the 3-D Sculpture Park artist residency program in Switzerland and AHL Foundation Residency in New York.
 
Cho’s works are featured in major collections such as Seoul Municipal Museum and Musée Cantonale des Beaux-Arts du Valais in Switzerland, and in  such as ‘Nature’s Tempo’ at the Korean Cultural Services of New York, and ‘Going Green’ in conjunction with Queens Art Express in New York.  She is passionate about performance art, projects include ‘Sounds of Fragment: Ecological Dreams’ at the Nam June Park Art Center and Seoul Innovation Park.

Cho was born in and resides in Seoul, Korea, but was educated in Switzerland, UK and USA.  She holds a BA and MFA from the Slade School of Fine Art in London and an MA in Art Education from Columbia University, by which she recently was honored with the Teacher’s College Medal for Distinguished Service. After obtaining her MFA, she taught visual art courses as well as theory at universities in Korea.

bio: Hello. I'm Jimin Lim, an artist from Korea. My work is inspired by the absence of my dad. After my dad passed away, I became extremely unstable, which made me often look through family photos with deep longing for the past. Unlike the dark time during my dad's fight against the disease, my family looked very happy in the photos. It seemed very familiar, yet distant. I interpret these moments into painting. I paint fragmented parts of the photos zoomed into people’s hands. Sometimes, through an absence, you feel the presence. Likewise, the cropped parts on canvas will stimulate your imagination even more. Thank you.

bio:
My workform follows an expressionist style, but is more like Naive Art in secret.Naive art is a unique style that expresses simple but intense emotions. I think that when I unravel my work in an intuitive and emotional way without using complex techniques, the message contained in it can be conveyed more directly. This is because when I am influenced by Naive art in works such as "Happy Woman Chun Shim-i", the truth and purity of the emotion can stand out and form a deep connection with the viewers.

Happiness is at the center of my work. It does not mean only grand achievements or brilliant moments. Rather, I would like to capture small moments of joy, small but deep resonant emotions that suddenly rise in everyday life.In particular, I pay attention to the happiness of women living today. Even in the eyes of the world and the expectations of their roles, women tend to live their lives in their own way and discover precious moments. When they smile, when they open their hearts sincerely, the smile that blooms like a flower is the most beautiful scenery I want to capture on the canvas.The figure in the painting makes eye contact with the viewer with a bright expression, as if she became one among the flowers. Her smile is not just a facial expression, but a testament to deep-rooted joy. A tiny but powerful happiness sustains life, sometimes just like the moment when you smile in a mirror while wearing your favorite clothes on a sunny day.To record these brilliant moments of women, I continue to paint. I hope that the smile, the eyes, will reach the viewers with a calm comfort and warmth...

I'm a musician and artist. I've been involved in film and drama production since 2007 as an entertainment promoter.

It is a work of art that invigorates success. We always want a happy life. We think every day about money, honor, health, stable family, work, old age, death, and planning for a loving family. Everyone does their best. After planning and pushing, you need to have good luck to get the best results. Enjoy lucky artworks, such as adding a spoonful of salt to plausible food. Yes, that's right. It's an organic painting!
What kind of painting do you want?
My paintings will contribute to your rich life and success, and they're paintings on the outside, though,
What I really express is to make your living space and environment pleasant without disturbing your dreams and hopes, and to maintain or improve your environment so that you don't lose what you have,
I want to continue to help you and your family increase their luck and achieve true success. I want to present happiness that I will cherish even after the painting is completed. I want to live a long human life and provide satisfaction and memories by creating a space where I can feel a sense of stability under any circumstances. You are the main character of the drama in your life.
I look forward to your successful life. Thank you ♡

bio:
Kyung-hee, Byun have held eleven solo exhibitions and participated in over 40 group exhibitions and art projects. Currently, Kyung-hee, Byun remain actively engaged in artistic practice.
The concept of Kyung-hee, Byun’s works began with the idea that when viewed from a distance, a person appears as a simple dot. Therefore, dots serve as an expression of human beings. While exploring the representation of people through divination, have pondered the true origin of that dot. Every individual is a singular entity, emerging from the intense competition for existence within the maternal womb. Life begins when we enter a vast world and leave our own distinct mark.
One could say that every great structure—even the universe itself—begins with a single dot. Thus, at its essence, everything originates from a solitary dot. And within each dot lies its own spirit and reason for existence.

bio:
The moment deprivation disappeared, life collapsed into emptiness.
 An endless darkness engulfed me, and as I fell beyond the bottom into deeper depths, I was consumed by pain.
 The darkness swallowed me, until I became the darkness itself. It spread beyond me, expanding outward, devouring everything around.
 There, I let go of everything.
 
 Yet paradoxically, within that endless darkness, I found a revelation. In the place where all had collapsed, I survived once again.
 
 Life often drifts within an indescribable emptiness, yet even within it, a subtle resonance remains. That resonance became the origin of my work.
 The colors and lines upon the canvas stand in place of the inner traces that language cannot contain.
 Through them, I confront my past, test my present, and seek my future.
 My paintings are not definitive answers, but fragments of questions that continue to unfold.

bio:
Hello, I'm a self-taught artist.  

Currently, I work as a 3D illustrator and pattern designer.
Combining various patterns and 3D arts in my digital works, I infuse my diverse imagination into my creations.

I often collaborate with AI to explore more diverse artistic possibilities.

I remember when I was young, my mom used to draw Barbie faces for me frequently. Everything seemed fascinating to my young eyes,

and I remember staring at the eyes she drew for a long time. That's when my interest in drawing began. Some of my relatives were artists, and I vividly recall going to an art supply store with them, buying sketchbooks, and practicing drawing by observing various objects.

In elementary school, I won my first art award, and in middle school, my interest in drawing grew as I enjoyed watching cartoons and sketching during breaks and lunchtime. I immersed myself in drawing, sketching fashion designs day and night, nurturing my dream of becoming a fashion designer. However, due to family circumstances, I had to move to another country, which momentarily halted my dedication to drawing.

Yet, through the process of learning and growing in life, 
I rediscovered my passion for drawing and began pursuing it once again.

bio:
Artist Wonmi Seo describes her painting practice as the formation of disassembly. Based in Seoul, South Korea, her studio sees collage, drawing and painting practices regularly combined into one, creating artworks both inspired by and in reaction to traditional painting practices throughout history. Exploring the overarching theme of death, Wonmi deftly articulates tenebrism and tactual methodologies to execute artworks that are beautiful conceptually as well as superficially.
​

Wonmi received her BFA in Painting from Sungkungkwan University, South Korea. She has won several awards for her work including the SDU Art Prize in 2018, and a Creative Support Scholarship from the Seoul Foundation for Arts and Culture. She has exhibited her works in group shows across Seoul, and had her first solo exhibition at Artspace Boan1942 in 2017.
​

bio:
Artist, Painter HyunJu Kim

‘Fruits Paradise’was created from my desire for an abundant world and my longing for making the impossible possible. It is the space which may correspond to the Peach-Blossom Garden of the oriental or a Paradise of the occidental. It is a place abundance which everyone dreams of.‘Aspiration’to escape from an insipid daily life;‘Imagination’induced from the aspiration, and;‘Desire’of a man longing for a rest and a happy life. Fruits, which often refer to‘freshness and life’, are, in my paintings, the projection of the aforesaid 3 factors. That is why the fruits in Fruits Paradise are fresher and more splendid than any other fruits in the secular world, and that is why they brightly glitters. Fruits Paradise is the place filled with vibrant energy of life pouring out from our never-ending aspiration and desire. It is my wish that all viewers of my paintings shall ‘take a rest and play around at’ Fruits Paradise, filled with the vibrant energy, while imagining the freshness pouring out from a bite of these lush fruits in my works.

Creation of Fruits Paradise
‘Fruits Paradise’series is rooted on Korean traditional paintings not only in the respect of psychological basis, but also in the respect of inspiration and way of creation. As I was majoring in oriental painting, I have taken courses related to Korean traditional paintings including the History of Oriental Painting, the History of Korean Painting, and the Oriental Aesthetics. These courses made me proud of Korean traditional paintings, as well as made me question myself what the aesthetical value of Korea in true sense would be. The answer that I came up so far is that what is genuinely Korean is the most global. Hence, I truly enjoy appreciating old paintings of Korea, and the Korean traditional paintings also have given me a lot of idea and inspiration. Accordingly, applying‘Jeon-Tong-Jin-Chae (Korean traditional colouring)’method, with which Korean traditional materials are used and traditional colouring techniques are followed, is one of important factors of my works. Smooth and clean silk is selected, and mounted on a wooden frame.‘Gyobansu (solution of traditional hide glue and alum)’ was made via sophisticated and tricky process, and applied on the front and back of the silk over and over more than 10 times to make an adequate foundation for painting. Drawing is done with oriental ink on this foundation, and traditional colours made from natural pigments mixed in hide glue solution are applied one by one. This process of creation gives traditional strong colour tone and at the same time, soft, thick and warm sensation, and this is why I choose it as the most effective way to describe a paradise. To depict the splendid, clear and strong impression of the fruits in my works, prime colours and loud colours are frequently used. Outstanding expression of colours, long duration without discoloration and maintaining high chroma when mixed, all of which are the basic requirements of oriental painting, are also important factor that I am focused on to enhance the aesthetic value of my works.

bio:
I make scultures and mixed media paintings by exploring transcendental and sacred themes, such as death, the universe, creation, and extinction. My creative process often begins with imagining intangible concepts that cannot be seen or experienced in the physical world, but can be understood through each person's inner intuition. I strive to explore the relationship between grotesque elements and spaces that evoke anxiety in the viewer, utilizing visual language such as dark colors, stones, and threat to achieve a visual impact.

The shapes and textures of stones, the timelessness of time and the sense of infinity they convey stand out in my work. In order to infuse a lasting sense of mystery and depth into my work, I actively utilizes the characteristics of stone such as permanence, depth, and sublimity. One of my enduring interests is exploring the boundary between reality and fantasy. Because of this, I enjoy creating visual confusion by creating an inappropriate combination of artificial media and natural objects that may seem somewhat unrealistic.

My art is an expression of my deepest beliefs and feelings, and an exploration of an intangible and limitless aspect of life that goes beyond our immediate sensory experience. Through my work, I hope to stimulate thoughts and emotions and give a glimpse of the transcendent realm that exists within all of us.

bio: There are things that cannot be fully expressed through language or writing. I put things in pictures that cannot be expressed in words or writing alone. My emotions and thoughts are piled up in the picture along with my memories, the present and my future path. I feel that these are not just my stories. The stars in the sky and the flowers of the earth hold and dream, I am in them. I learn the secrets one by one. The pain and what I learned from overcoming it. Hopes and dreams bloom as a single flower in the picture. I think life is like the flower of love blooming. I hope that each flower blooms.

rreonsu (Yeonsoo) is a contemporary painter whose work delves into the intricate cycle of human expectation, longing, and persistence. Selected as a featured artist for Samsung Art TV, her practice has gained international recognition for its unique blend of organic abstraction and philosophical depth.

Using oil and mixed media, rreonsu visualizes socially constructed standards—the "good life" and "good person"—through the proliferation of organic forms such as cells, roots, and fungi. Her "Gaze" series captures the movement of sensation, transitioning from broad environmental awareness to intimate, magnified focus.

Her work is an intuitive record of moments where the gaze lingers, inviting viewers to reconsider their own expectations from a spacious, liberated perspective. Based in South Korea, rreonsu continues to push the boundaries of her materials, creating a "gaze full of longing" that resonates with collectors seeking both aesthetic beauty and conceptual resonance.

Inspired by childhood memories and nature, her paintings invite viewers into lush, intimate worlds filled with rich color and delicate detail.

Using custom-made palette knives, she builds layered oil paintings with vivid textures and movement.

Her works are collected for their emotional depth and calming yet vibrant presence.

bio:
I am an artist based in Korea. I have been working with a character called “Moony.” Moony is a character I created during my childhood, and since my university years, I have continuously expanded Moony’s world and narrative.

The name “Moony” means “to shine like the moon,” embodying a pure heart that glows softly like moonlight, along with the chubby and adorable appearance of a young child.

In my current work, Moony characters each create their own happy lives, and I capture their memories—formed through individual spaces and moments in time—within my artworks
