bio:
On the Familiarity of the Alien


My works are drawn from different manifestations of nature such as aspects of trees, plants and common landscapes to which we usually pay little or no attention. Sometimes we can experience the boundary between the real and the ideal through single-pointed concentration free of conceptual thought.
We are surrounded by many things of which we are not consciously aware. Sometimes even everyday things and situations can seem alien to us. This may be because we simply do not notice their presence or fail to dwell on their existence.
Human beings are defined by their interdependent relationship with other human beings and their environments. Sometimes we are aware of this and sometimes we are not. This is the essence of Oriental philosophy and the source of all vitality. When we lose this awareness we are drained of energy, but when we regain it our strength returns. The spirit of the era and the state of the environment determine our destiny. Therefore, we must never ignore even trivial, little things that give meaning to our lives. It is these alien - yet familiar - perceptions that I endeavor to integrate into my work. Sometimes I try to capture the motion and structure of things as well as the passing of time with my brush strokes. This aspect of my work grants me insight into the natural harmony that pervades all existence. It is this which is required to transcend distracted consciousness and to realize the boundlessness of space.
All my work is based on the experience of being on or going beyond these boundaries. It is a dialogue with our environment and a discourse on existence, which ultimately leads back to familiarity.
                                                             Pyo Youngyong (Artist)

bio:
I am Heejae Kim, a painter who has dedicated over 60 years to the canvas. My artistic identity is defined by the world’s first pioneering 'Knife Painting' technique, through which I carve layers of time and contemplation rather than simply applying color.

My work explores a dialectical aesthetic where void meets vitality, and extinction gives rise to creation. From the deep abyss of darkness, I bring forth the resilient energy of pale green life and ethereal moonlight, capturing the essence of existence that shines even in solitude.

Building upon my academic foundations at Chung-Ang University and École des Beaux-Arts in Paris, I invite you to join my journey—a silent, meditative path that blurs the boundaries between the earthly and the celestial.

Artist Kim Incheol is great interested in the "Dot". It is one of basic element in the formative arts. He trusted that the Dot has sufficient formative language by itself and expressed a unique visual as the differential or integral on formative elements. The Dot is a group of another dots, each Dots become again component parts to form different shape. As a matter of course, the Dot can change with perfect freedom because it is the smallest unit of formative element. The Dots filled on a canvas make rhythm themselves and it becomes a method giving rise to the expansion of consciousness from spectators too. Recently his works are showing that the material of Dot is not limited to draw on the canvas and based on all formations instead of occupying physical space. The work to dot and build small tactile points in full details with acrylic painting is very simple and requires much concentration. In this way, it is similar with Zen Buddhism to form of the buddhist religion that concentrates on mention. If the foundation of abstract in the art put the accent on elaborate recognition about reality, his works reflects deep interest and faith about formative basic principles.

bio: 1967/Masan in KoreaWorks by eclectic painter Young Zoo You seem to transcend boundaries of style and subject matter, resisting easy classification. Combining disparate styles and cultural worldviews, Young Zoo You crafts highly imaginative paintings using mixed media, oil, or acrylic. His messages are conveyed by the use of emotive symbols, some bizarre and playful, others astute and timeless. He makes use of his knowledge of many greats of art history, particularly Van Gogh, co-opting and combining elements in order to create new meaning for our times. We find epic battles for the fate of the universe, complex architectural forms full of inhabitants rising toward the skies, and goddesses cloaked in computer code. Young Zoo You favors robust color schemes and highly complex geometric patterns. Dipping into and selecting references to pop culture, art and world history allows for a universal dialogue based on our shared social history that truly transcends national boundaries. I can contemplate the movement of my heart best in the process of the endless repetition of painting, he says.Young Zoo You lives and works in Busan, South Korea.

bio: Armed with a sense of irony and love of serendipity, John intends to fight the coming darkness by encouraging awesomeness.

[Artist's Note]
Scientific progress of the cutting-edge technology changed the personal relationship in diverse and complex way by the use of social networking services.
Nevertheless, it is not easy to communicate honestly in the midst of the overflowing superficial relationships.
Furthermore people fall into the abyss of misfortune due to damaged relationships.

Still, if there is someone who I can share the warmth of the body... if there is someone who stands by me withstanding all the hardships,
the World would be so much better place to live.

[Art Critic review]

By Viviana Puello, Editor in Chief – ArtTour International Magazine

“Young-Ae Yi is a South Korean artist that has proven her express understanding of pain. Additionally her work displays the constant battle that humans face between laughter and tears. Young-Ae Yi appears to be extremely well versed in the area of human comedy, drama, pain and laughter. She is able to intelligently convey and mix beginning innocence with cathartic representation and ageless wisdom. Her raw artistic skills were developed by way of intimate experience. The rather vivid imagery of this artist provides viewers of the compositions with a feeling of endless possibility.
The naïve yet heart capturing style of this artist affords those that gaze upon her works to believe in the world’s possibilities once again. The artistic works of Young-Ae Yi tend to be tale of vibrantly warm colors that overflow with the internal battle offerings of the human spirit.
Young-Ae Yi has been able to distill a universally received antidote that has been created of expressly optimistic imagery. Somehow she is able to understand that the planet is highly affected by pessimism yet yearning for the opposing effect. It is that opposing effect that needed optimism that her works are able to provide viewers with consistently. Her conveyance is not juvenile or out of the far reach of reality. It is actually rooted within a reality that is shroud in pain and discourse. Her works remind us all that there is beauty within all things, especially vibrantly alluring color. As one takes in her compositions, they are allowed to escape to their time in life before they were tainted by the world. A time when all seems within reach. When life seemed filled of mystery, wonder, joy and possibility.
Through the eyes and artistry of the incomparable Young-Ae Yi, we are all reminded that the world is our oyster. Through pain and through triumph, there is also an occasion for a smile.”

Read full article at the ArtTour International Magazine 2015 Spring Issue

bio:
An abyss nestled on the deep edge inside such a profound cave.

In that place is ‘an abyss’ figuratively meaning a pit hard to escape from.
An abyss which is completely void, or is void but is not void anywhere and so is fully filled. In such space, I  reach the beginning of the universe, that is, the time of the creation of the world which puts together the truth of the universe, life or death, energy, wave, quark, and time-space. Both substance and non-substance are images full of simulacre, from which works created by me are not also any different.
‘’I‘’ or ‘myself’ exist in the earth here as a three-dimensional planet which high-dimensional self has chosen, and also the direction and will of my life exists now and here by the will which has tried to experience all the spots of life in person.
Perhaps, even though this opportunity is not the first time but has been sustained throughout several lives, all the things which I live, breathe, and think now are emitted into wave and energy deep in the universe. That’s right. Only as long as I exist, my telepathy goes through the universe.
A tiny existence like a grain of sand has experienced eternal time and space to pull up the mind of gratitude and love from an abyss inside deep heart. This is the sympathy and unity between the whole existence(void) and myself(zero point). Through this, I think of the truth and existence of the universe anew.
Although I still walk the same road as that of yesterday, now I create another day and am emitted into another energy and wave.
What I expressed is also the very energy and wave in the back of such abyss as if I, who had existed in the past as her, him, or energy in the air, had done do.
What did you see, feel, and think? What was you impressed with? You could find nothing from colors and materials which appear ostensibly. If you can see yourself anywhere inside a very gaping abyss you will feel deep sympathy with the whole existence(void), and ultimately find all the emotions having pursued by you until now.

 Jiwon choi tries to experience a whole moment, even though not perfect, through painting. On a screen, she puts colors and brush marks at an adequate place to form a shape. This process is called 'The imagination of the rise of supernumerary rainbow and its explosion'. The supernumerary rainbow, which describes a situation of multiple rainbows rising at the same time, occurs only when the size of all the raindrops are the same and smaller than usual. Then, a sunlight is reflected inside the raindrops and creates colors of a rainbow. Whereabouts of the colors in the screen are at such exquisite spots. She believes in the situation after the explosion of the supernumerary rainbow. She records the air like a hyaline mirror and the experience of the clear present through painting.

bio: ChaeWon Moon (b.1992, Korea) is a visual artist living and working in  South Korea. Her practice focuses on the inevitable failure behind order and rule; sensing nonsense from the organized logic is a central idea of her practice. She borrows pictures and texts from manuals and reassembles them into a non-functional system. The work reflects her interest in the tension between order and playful illegibility, and also ambivalence caused by this conflict. She constructs the rebus that refused to decoded. Her work reads as dark humor about attempts to control the situation that only need an ideal result from the process. By deconstructing and rebuilding the structure of the manual, which is designed to point the answer or the goal, she parodies familiarity and perfection. In her work, the structure that supposed to present a concrete and helpful solution becomes a tool to address the intended misunderstanding.

Hi

Since I was boy, I've suffered and faced a lots of situations and problems such as family problems, money problems, education problems.. something made me depressed.

So i always alone but I've inspired from that such as loneliness, depressive, violence and narcissism and also I've thought about the essential things about our world. Essence of our existence something philosophical thoughts. All of things which I felt or thought from my life have been my inspirations for my works. I inspired from myself. It can be say like that. I know I also just little foolish living thing which want to know about essential of universe but if I going to live on like this I could be make a smile when I face the death.



Nowadays artist who called themselves 'artist', they think too easily about art and also they just use their works for the portfolio. They make their sketches, paintings, drawings even notes about their feelings or thoughts. So I feel they just do the art for their uni or something like own profits. I know and admire their passions but I want to say that passions is not for the essential of the art. Think about something new and creative things are also important to art but most nowadays artist focus on only that. That is just one side of the art...



And also I think as the art can't be educated from other people because we live on in each individual universe. So you can't feel same things as others. To sum up, professors have no right to evaluate young artists works.



I just want to show the world about essential of the art so even now I try to search that.

You who have suffered, focus on my works and just have deep breath and feel yourself

bio:
My inner world is in constant motion, endlessly mixing and shifting within its own confusion.
When I paint, ink and paper intertwine, the strokes merging irreversibly into one another. At times, even the paper itself seems to move. Then comes a moment when intention can no longer intervene, and all that remains is to witness the unfolding change.

Like yin and yang, my paintings find harmony between necessity and chance, taking on their own shapes and colors.
This reminds me of life itself—of human existence—imperfect yet beautiful in its way. Our will, mingling with countless uncontrollable variables, continues to form a certain shape as it moves forward.

Jun sung Back is a Korean artist who represents the original voice of contemporary art. He creates original visual experiences through colorful colors and bold compositions, and his works artistically embody human emotions and social issues that can be found in everyday life. His artistic journey has crossed the boundaries between the real world and imagination, and he has built his own unique world of work through various mediums and techniques.

One of his major works, the "Walking" series and the "lucky box" series, are his representative works, which impress viewers through their sensual harmony of colors and forms, offering a new perspective on everyday activities. 

The "Lucky Box" series is based on the joy and excitement that began with the children's comprehensive gift set that I received every holiday during my childhood. The anticipation filled with the box while wondering what was inside the wrapping paper at that time, and the happiness I felt when I opened the gift will never be forgotten over time.

Through this series, I wanted to remind you of the pure joy and hope of that childhood. Today, we forget many things in our daily lives, but I hope that my paintings will come to me like a gift and convey small and precious happiness. "Lucky Box" is more than just a work, it was born out of a desire to present the joy and warmth that can be felt in life.

Jun sung Back has showcased his works at several domestic and international art fairs and exhibitions, receiving great acclaim. His works have been recognized not only in Korea but also on the world stage, and he has been invited to several international art exhibitions and biennials, and has won numerous awards. In particular, he was selected as the cover artist of "The best of Watercolor" for the first time in East Asia on Splash 22 in the United States, which attracted attention. His works are housed in several major galleries and institutions, including the National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul City Hall, and the War Memorial of Korea, and are highly regarded among art enthusiasts. 

The artist seeks to communicate through art, and his works provide visitors with new visual experiences and opportunities for deep contemplation. He continues to create and push the boundaries of contemporary art, and he will continue to inspire many people in the future.

bio:

The theme of  my work is " recovery " and "healing" and I really would like to give hope and joy to a lot of heart people  from my artwork.
With the deep inspiration of oriental painting, I am creating my own unique and unique painting work that is oriental and Western by combining the beauty of the margins of oriental painting, the method of expressing all emotions with one brush, and the essence of objects with lines and dots. Through life like "Tae-jeom," it took natural materials and turned them into works of joy in life. There are also times when we can miss peace when we experience hard times in a city. At that time, I looked at the sky and clouds and meditated on everything that did not change, expressed it with the material of nature and expressed the garden of life.

I am a South Korean artist whose work oscillates between abstraction and painterly expression. My paintings often explore themes of identity, inner conflict, and the tension between nature and the human psyche. Using bold yet restrained tones, I seek to evoke both emotional depth and philosophical reflection in the viewer.

While I have a strong connection to my cultural roots, I also strive to speak a universal visual language that resonates beyond borders. Each canvas I approach is a negotiation between the seen and the unseen, the controlled and the instinctual.

Personal Revelation Through Illness – A Near-Death Experience as Artistic Awakening (2024)
After a life-threatening illness brought me to the threshold of death, the dormant seed of art that had quietly existed within me since childhood began to stir—like the beanstalk in a fairytale, breaking through the ordinary, growing wild and inevitable. This moment reshaped my existence and redirected my path wholly toward art, where I now explore the borderlands of emotion, fragility, and life itself.

Acting Studies and the Unfulfilled Dream (2020-2021)
After graduating with a degree in Architectural Design, I took a detour to pursue my childhood dream of becoming a film actor. Though I never appeared on screen, the immersive training in acting and movement profoundly shaped my artistic path. It deepened my emotional language and led me to explore the body, gesture, and presence—elements that now breathe within my visual work.

Lives and works in Paju

Kyungmin Lee is a contemporary artist based in Korea, whose work continuously explores the concepts of light, space, and boundaries. Graduating with a degree in Art Practice from Goldsmiths University in the UK in 2012, Lee experiments with new aesthetic experiences that transcend the boundaries of nature and artifice, time and space, the individual and the collective. His work focuses on visualizing spatial and sensory experiences rooted in geopolitical boundaries. Specifically, his time in the military, experiencing life in a border region, and his interactions with North Korean people during his studies in the UK became key moments that allowed him to view the reality of division in a new light. Drawing inspiration from physical and conceptual boundaries such as the DMZ, South Korean propaganda broadcasts, and military spaces, he expands the meaning of boundaries through the interplay of light, sound, white and yellowing, material and data. Through changes in light and surface, he reveals the uncertainty of boundaries and explores invisible power structures and the flow of information through the echoes and distortions of sound.

Lee's work is rooted in the political and social contexts he has experienced, delving into the complex interactions within boundaries. The colors and shapes in his works are not just visual elements; they serve as important vehicles for communicating the intersections between his inner world and the external world. Living near the DMZ and hearing South Korean propaganda broadcasts daily still plays a crucial role in his work, with past and present experiences blending naturally into his creations. Through his military service, he experienced tension with North Korea, and during his studies in the UK, his encounters with North Korean people reshaped his understanding of the reality of division. He continues to explore and visualize these experiences through color and form.

bio:
Rooted in the quiet philosophies of East Asia, I create artworks that reflect a longing for inner peace and emotional grounding. My journey as an artist began from a place of restlessness—a search for balance in an overwhelming world. Over time, I turned to the ancient traditions of East Asian painting, learning to grind my own ink and to paint with pigments derived from nature.

In my studio, silence is not empty — it is full of presence. I work surrounded by calming scents and gentle sounds, aligning my senses with each brushstroke. The process itself is a ritual: an intimate harmony between body, breath, and canvas.

Through each piece, I hope to pass on the serenity and quiet energy that I have found. My work is not just for myself — it is for those who pause in front of it. I want my art to be like a breath: a moment of stillness, a soft reminder that beauty can be found in stillness and simplicity.

May each painting bring to its viewer the same sense of calm and vitality that it brings to me.

bio:
I am a painter who expresses the hard life of a busy modern man cheerfully.

Having dreamed of becoming a cartoonist since childhood, I decided to become an artist since I loved the artist's life and works of art I saw in an artist's studio.

Afterwards, I learned the paintings with my neighbor's painters and won a special prize in the 27th Korean Art Exhibition Planning Division in 2008, and displayed it at the National Museum of Modern Art.

I've been doing fine art work mainly using ink pens since the beginning.
Acrylic, oil markers, watercolor paper, canvas, cotton fabrics and panels are used as materials.
I use the unique properties of different materials to find the color that suits my art style.
I also like to sculpt character characters from paintings and paint on them.
On behalf of Canbis, we are making sculptures using compressed styrofoam, earthenware, and wood materials.

My work has visually impressive features in the world.
Many people think that money is the standard of success in a capitalist society.
Owning a large house in Korea is a symbol of wealth.
However, I don't think money is all about happiness.
Many people make money by running hard to get rich, but maybe we can be happy even if there is only one house where my family can be comfortable.

I would like to be able to look back at our life once more by seeing people being made of human forms with buildings filled in my paintings.

bio:
Yoojin Kim's practice begins with the transformation of discarded objects into new forms of vitality. In her work, familiar things are not remnants stripped of function, but rediscovered as a "medium of possibility" — surfaces on which emotion and form can accumulate. Reconstructed into unpredictable, organic shapes through repetitive connection, her sculptures create an illusion of movement, revealing a presence that feels alive and breathing.

Her process begins with improvisational, unconscious impulse and evolves into a search for the meaning latent within emotion. Here, material functions not merely as an extension of physical matter, but as an emotional organ — drawing to the surface fragments of depression, anxiety, fear, and sorrow. The object transforms into a passage between the unconscious and the external world, carrying within it the weight of inner feeling.

In her recent work, Yoojin explores the structure through which interior emotion condenses and expands into a living form. The organ-like mass at the center symbolizes the core of destructive emotion that long troubled the artist, while the tentacles extending outward embody the simultaneous expression of the will to survive and the instinct to reach beyond. Soft curves and layered textures reveal this duality, capturing the moment when emotion finds form through sublimation.

Yoojin Kim's sculptures exist as neither organism nor object — visualizing the process by which discarded things, suppressed emotions, and invisible unconscious forces are converted into new life. Through this, the artist blurs the boundary between life and art, interior and exterior, inviting viewers to encounter familiar objects and emotions from an entirely new perspective.

bio:
Ghosting"”What Lies Hidden Under the After-image

Diogenes"”still remembered as the man who said to Alexander the Great, "I would like you not to block the sun""”has taught us to defy all convention; to not lose our self dignity; and to find our happiness in our inner, not outer, world. He yearned for a pure, anarchist state of being and tried to make people realize that conventions and traditions, such as laws and systems, are mere bubbles. His world view can be defined, in a nutshell, by the Greek word "kynic." The term refers to a "pleasure-seeking anarchist skeptic," but one who should not be a cynic. Such attitude, surprisingly, overlaps with the artistic phenomena taking place in our time: the convention-defying avant-garde spirit; art that is armored with attitude rather than form; protest against conventional beliefs and systems; the gesture of spitting at the world; meaningless pleasures; and nevertheless, an attitude of pluralism, that last bastion which at least keeps us from turning cynical, maintaining tolerance for the traits and sensibilities of others. Such phenomena define post-modernism. In this sense, the Diogenesian spirit is a distant ancestor of post-modernism. 

Kim Dong-jin's paintings are also trees that have been nursed by the waters of a Diogenesian spring. His artistic journey, which began in 1991, was one headed towards the fringe, embracing things that no one bothered to look at. Kim turned away from what was mainstream or powerful or muscular, famous, expensive or trendy, as well as all that others longed to possess and to acquire"”what people found beautiful, irresistible, sweet, hedonistic, splendid or orderly"”and instead, pulled to his side and made strictly his own all that was on the other end. He dug up nostalgia from old forgotten posters of rural villages and brought to the center stage used machine parts that had been brutally abandoned. He loved stale, soggy cookies rather than sweet, crispy biscuits. He preferred the grotesque ugliness of an old man's dentures to the balance created by a pair of beautiful breasts. By denying the conceptual system of what others believe to be right or good, Kim developed an aethestics of negation and discovered an even stronger life force from death imagery, rather than from life imagery. The following is an entry from Kim's journal towards the end of his journey to the fringe during the 1990s:

"Death is the most terrible thing of all, and the greatest strength is demanded to keep death's work going." Hegel's statement is both the starting point and the destination of my meditation. The highest force is perhaps located on two polar ends. Men reach a stage of transcendence only when they overcome the pain of death. Only when they taste death they begin to understand life's high moments. My companions, or my codes, wander the vicinity of death and indifference, isolation and the fringe. This realm of death and isolation is where I discover my infinite high moments in life. 

As we can see above, Kim Dong-jin's "companions," or "codes," were the forces of life that occurred on a seemingly helpless and vulnerable being's path to recovery after overcoming death. It was an attempt to overturn conventional ideas while building his own ideas"”just as a small shrub can absorb light and rainwater only when a big tree falls. It was not until the late 2000s, however, that Kim finally accepted that attitude alone cannot give life to a new art form. It was only then that he was able to realize, art is no different from liquor, brewed from a mixture of attitude, form, and metaphor. He came to reconsider his aethestics of negation, which no one admired, and instinctively learned that his itinerary had to be altered. It was none other than the word honesty that had brought him to his knees. What is it that I love the most? What is the goal of my artistic pursuit? What is art?

Kim had always been a fan of cartoons and movies. When alone, he would drift amidst these rich yet light images. In these moments, he would feel no pain, and realized that this is a sensibility shared by the rest of his generation. For a long time, he contemplated the differences between film, including animation, and painting, the oldest medium around. For Kim, it was in these streaming images, such as film or animation, where he was able to maintain a sense of painless ease and serenity, but he found no comfort when it came to the overbearing obligations and physical constraints that painting imposed"”the medium of painting demanded that he discover something wholly new. In 2008, Kim reached a bold resolution after struggling with the traits of his generation, his memories of the past, and the obligations posed by the genre of painting. From 1996 to the 2000s, he tried to create astriking contrast of light and dark, and dynamicstructures. Recently his screen gradually becamealmost black all over. Basic circular structures werehinted by the visible traces of light and dark shadingof dots, or margins between them. He often ordered thesections of visual masses with vertical, horizontaland curved lines. Meanwhile, his work was movingtowards an analogy of traditional Korean styles. Currently, his work, shown in his 9th solo exhibition,held at the Joseon Daily Newspaper Art Museum inSeoul, clearly indicated different issues which are acontinuation of his experimental trajectory, and whichwill be freshly explored in the 2000s. This was, Ithought, the highlight of this exhibition. His recent work can be described as an image ofarchaeological rhizome, which is the title of thisessay. In other words, these terms are the base on, orroot from, which Lee Seong Ku has generated hisimages. This indicates that the artist wants toestablish his vision of the world in a deeper realm,not on the surface of the natural world or in mentalimages. Until now, the artist termed such a profoundrealm as Nature. However, there is a strong needto articulate this more explicitly, in terms of thearchaeological rhizome. The rhizome is anoriginally botanical term, referring to a root likemutated subterranean stem, shooting out sub-branchesunder the ground that produce small roots. The stemsof Bamboo and lotus are the typical examples of this.Rhizome, here, in Lee Seong Kus work, means thatthe artist wishes his images to be, not like the upperbranches of the plant above the soil, but like thelower branches beneath the soil, shooting out manysmall roots, in order to connect with the one originalsource. In this respect, his work can be described asarchaeological, meaning that it searches for theorigin. The artist who wishes his work to be anarchaeological rhizome should view the inner natureof Nature and traditional Korean notion of naturalnessas being the same. According to the artists ownterms: I humbly tried to recover traditional Koreancharacteristics through connecting my study of acondensed expression containing thoughts on the originof myriad things in the natural world and on the innernature of Nature, to commonplace forms and colours.(From the artists note)The quotation above suggests that the artistunderstood rhizome as the original quality ofnaturalness that we can find in Korean naturalenvironment and traditional styles, and at the sametime, as the power that transcends space and time.From this point, we notice another approach in his newworking methods. Until now, the artist has tried toconnect the mental images to the rhizome, which isviewed as the original source of naturalness. He triedto find the connecting point of the mental images andthe rhizome in re-interpreting absorbing and smudgingeffects of ink. Absorbing and smudging effects of ink are the naturalitself. If I tried to generate the expressivesubstance of the mental images, composed within thetime and spatial limitations, through the variationsof these effects, this will be a natural beauty, andstronger than any artificial results. bio:
The Gorgeous City! 
The theme of his work at the exhibition is 'City of Fire.' Inspired by the work he happened to see at the Hong Kong Art Festival, he says he wanted to paint on these themes one day. 

 Each of the crowds in his works is wearing colorful clothes and posing in an unknown. At first glance, it looks like a dancing singer, or a model to be on the stage in fancy clothes. It's up to the viewers to interpret the work, but they definitely have their own energy and individuality. The same is true of the modern society in which we live. In particular, a group of individuals is likely to have one unified goal and their individuality is ignored, but the group is eventually a group of individuals with different personalities. This individuality is further influenced by individual dreams, hopes, and aspirations.

 The colorful lights in the work depict the individual colors of each of us living in a colorful city, and use strong colors to exude the energy that was inherent in each person. Dynamic dance moves, intense colors. They are bringing together to complete a dynamic and colorful scene of the city. 

 Why are they showing off their dynamic gestures under colorful lights? Why did the writer take The Gorgeous City as the theme? With curiosity, he wanted to find the answer. 

 Of course, you can find the reason in the above commentary, but in another sense, the emotions of modern people's anguish, frustration, sadness and anger hidden in the city that glows splendidly without distinction of day and night are hidden in dynamic dance moves and intense colors. If each person's ideas, values, and personalities in one group are not respected, they will struggle to break away from the group or demand a change in the group. Although it looks splendid on the outside, looking inside, it appears that they have shaped such works to show the people who struggle fiercely in the city filled with darkness and scars. He is showing them in a dramatic and dynamic way. His work, in this sense, leads the viewer to indulge in a variety of thoughts. 

There could be a degree of difference to understand his work. You can just take it with a strong sense of color, leave your body to a dynamic dance, or find your own meaning inside it. Just as many individual people gather and form a society, there is no fixed meaning in a painting, and the value of it will only be proved when various thoughts and values of a work form a story. 


 2018 July Hot Summer Day

 Cho Haeng-rim, a literary critic

bio:
Black shuts up light and makes the object’s original color disappear. The light obtained from white becomes the start of the narrative with the image. My artwork is also one of the innumerable individual narratives. My story is about a family that started from marriage of couples. While the ordinary topics and ideas on taste of son, travel of father, and time of wife may derive empathy from many people, people might find them boring. I don’t want to care about it that much. My artwork involves natural acceptance of the fear of blurring boundaries from aging and attempt to feel the impression that couldn’t be felt because of the precise and skilled vision. Especially, I am interested in the color of light in the “Dawn”. The tuning for the whole at the moment right before emitting each color from the darkness shows something beyond senses and perfect balance that I sought throughout my artwork.   

- Artist’s Note-

bio:
Daedo Jun is an artist and researcher whose work explores human interiority, contemplative spirituality, and consciousness as lived experience.

Rather than explaining or defining the human condition, his practice seeks to create conditions in which one may quietly return to inner awareness. Grounded in theological reflection, contemplative practice, and philosophical inquiry, his approach emphasizes silence, attentiveness, and an inward reorientation of perception. His work invites stillness rather than argument, presence rather than explanation.

Alongside his artistic practice, Daedo Jun has published more than twenty research papers and scholarly essays across fields including AI studies, consciousness research, and spiritual philosophy. These works are archived in international research platforms such as OSF, PhilArchive, PhilPapers, Academia, and Zenodo, forming an ongoing dialogue between reflective inquiry and contemporary thought.

In parallel, he maintains a visual art practice that gives form to silence and inner light beyond language. His images do not demand interpretation; instead, they function as quiet surfaces through which viewers may encounter their own inner landscape. Abstraction and restraint are used not to obscure meaning, but to suspend it—allowing attention to settle before judgment or narrative takes hold.

His work consistently favors presence over explanation, stillness over persuasion, and depth over display. Through both writing and image, Daedo Jun continues a contemplative exploration of forms of expression that do not exhaust the human interior, but gently allow it to breathe.

Her art often explores themes of nature, identity, and cultural heritage, reflecting a profound connection to Korean traditions while embracing contemporary perspectives.

Lee Na-hyun has exhibited her work in numerous solo and group exhibitions both in South Korea and internationally. 

This introduction highlights Lee Na-hyun’s artistic style, themes, education, and achievements, providing a comprehensive overview of her contributions to the art world.

bio: Gyeongjin An is a Korean sculptor whose work is grounded in a sustained inquiry into the human condition. His practice began with figurative clay works and expanded into shadow and void-based pieces that delicately evoke emotion, memory, and absence. He later turned to spheres—the most essential units of form—as a way of exploring fluid identity and the temporality of being. Recently, his kinetic sculptures have sought to materialize meditative states through movement. An’s work reveals restrained emotional intensity and emphasizes sensation over narrative, emptiness over density, and transformation over fixity. This sensibility, rooted in Korean aesthetics yet articulated in a contemporary sculptural language, allows his to pose quiet yet profound questions about what it means to be human. He has held 15 solo exhibitions and participated in over 150 curated group shows in Korea and internationally.

bio:
I wanted to explore the inner self and emotions of humans through my work. The paintings created through my work are not simple portraits, but attempts to express the complex emotions and psychology of humans. The distorted and exaggerated features of the face, or the blurred or simply expressed features, contain the intention to reveal or conceal the true emotions that we hide in our daily lives.

The various colors and thick lines used in my works are tools to visually express the intensity of emotions. Primary colors such as red, blue, and yellow symbolize each emotional state. Red represents anger and passion, blue represents sadness and loneliness, and yellow represents joy and hope. The combination of these colors expresses the complexity and multi-layeredness of emotions.

I am very interested in the various emotions and psychological conflicts that humans experience in modern society. In particular, I want to express the loneliness and anxiety of modern people, and the hope and joy they find in it. These themes are deeply related to my personal experiences.

I am also greatly inspired by the works of expressionist and surrealist artists. Like their works, I focus on exploring the inner self of humans and expressing it visually.

The works created through my work reflect the emotional confusion and complexity that humans experience in modern society. We experience various emotions in our daily lives, but we have difficulty expressing them. The works that come from these experiences try to visually reveal such emotions, helping viewers recognize and empathize with their emotions. In addition, I wanted to emphasize that the expression of emotions is not simply personal, but a social and universal experience.

My work is part of a journey that explores the human mind and emotions. I tried to express the complexity and intensity of emotions through primary colors, thick lines, and distorted shapes. The ultimate goal of my work is to visually reveal the various emotional experiences we experience in modern society, helping viewers recognize and empathize with their emotions.

I hope that through my works, viewers can look into their own minds and discover the complexity and beauty of emotions. I think that art is not simply a pursuit of beauty, but a process of exploring the essence of humanity and understanding ourselves through it.

Artist Statement
In the fast-paced rhythm of modern urban life, people inevitably experience stress and seek healing in their own ways. Sometimes, even the effort to rest requires additional planning and time, which can itself become another source of pressure. For me, one of the most meaningful forms of healing is experiencing nature.

When I began my life as an artist, I developed an interest in gardening. As I observed the small flowers I grew through each changing season, I felt myself drawing closer to nature, and through that closeness, I experienced emotional restoration. I was fascinated by how each flower carried its own delicately refined design and unique palette of colors. Gradually, I found myself appreciating even the trees and grass along the streets, marveling at their transformations and vitality.

I sense the presence of nature in the subtle changes of the seasons—when I notice the shifting colors of leaves, when the wind brushes against my skin, or when I observe the quiet growth of a small potted plant. In those moments, I feel both fully alive and deeply present. These experiences gently return me to a forgotten world of childlike innocence, offering a sense of comfort and peace.

Human beings are also part of nature. When we see children running freely and joyfully, we often find ourselves smiling without realizing it—perhaps because we recognize and respond to that pure innocence. I believe that as long as we carry even a small piece of that purity within our hearts, we can endure difficult seasons. Like flowers that withstand the winter and bloom again in vibrant color, hope can always blossom anew.

Through my work, I seek to express the subtle transformations of the natural environment around me, intertwined with the innocent wonder I once felt while reading fairy tales as a child. Imagining stories through various characters is part of this process. Rather than dwelling on heavy or serious thoughts, I aim to create warm and gentle images that invite viewers into moments of lighthearted imagination. By using characters as emotional bridges, I strive to communicate vitality and life energy in a way that is intuitive and accessible, naturally sharing the sense of aliveness I feel through nature.

bio:
Hyun’s paintings depict the forest within our minds.
You will encounter electrifying and intense hues of the East in hyun's forest.

You will be instantly enveloped—drawn into the profound and intense forest she has created, a space that quietly captivates the heart and lingers within.

A forest—an inner space that carries the essence of seasons. As I wander through it, I feel the shifting seasons of my heart. In moments of solace, in moments of anger, my inner world is painted with ever-changing colors.
Hyun captures emotional landscapes through the unique softness yet intensity of East Asian pigments. In this particular piece, she conveys the stillness of deep green foliage and the trembling sound of crimson trees, burning like the fervent desires within. —Within these colors and movements, we come face to face with our own hearts.


The colors, created by layering East Asian pigments multiple times on resilient Hanji paper, possess a profound depth.
It is a time-consuming process that requires patience and dedication.

bio:
I have always been drawn to patterns — the invisible structures that give shape to complex systems. But it was my first drone flight over Australia that revealed nature's own version of that logic.
What began as a personal escape became a revelation: the earth, seen from above, is a world unto itself. The geometric channels of Western Australia's pink salt lakes. The fractal coastlines where turquoise ocean dissolves into white sand. The ancient, overwhelming mass of Uluru at dusk. These are not simply landscapes — they are the hidden logic of the natural world, readable only from the sky.
I am drawn to the tension between the overwhelming scale of nature and the unexpected order it reveals from a distance. Shooting with both drone and mirrorless camera, I pursue images that exist somewhere between photography and fine art — moments where the earth itself becomes the canvas, and distance becomes a new kind of clarity.

I am Junyi Heo(2002-birth), an artist based in South Korea.

In the past, socialization in our society aimed to cultivate a model human being. Winners were glorified as heroes, and individuals were taught to function as components within the vast machinery of society. In contrast, contemporary socialization superficially appears to adopt the opposite approach. Individuals are now expected to discover their self-identity and express absolute uniqueness. Yet, this expectation is soon transformed into images consumable within the market’s system of tastes, resulting in the redefinition of personal form under invisible norms cloaked by the rhetoric of freedom. In this process, “individuality” no longer signifies genuine difference. Instead, it becomes a competition of distinctiveness, an obsession with the necessity of being different.

Within this context, I have revisited the notion of individuality. It no longer represents true uniqueness, but rather the compulsion to be distinct. Thus, I seek the 眞我 (true self) or 本性 (innate nature), the primordial essence. My paintings are attempts to transplant classical painting grammar into contemporary narratives and experiments in juxtaposing temporal layers. The formal systems established in the works of René Sans and Neoclassicism have functioned not merely as stylistic conventions, but as “structural forms” symbolizing universal human concerns. I borrow the symbolic power of these structures to render the fractures of modern society visible on an otherwise invisible plane.

The stage within my canvases is constructed on the premise of “non-temporality.” Although it may appear to belong to a specific era, it is in fact a synthetic space that blurs temporal boundaries. Within this space, figures are arranged as mythic or allegorical symbols, metaphorically representing structural issues of contemporary society. Beneath the classical surface, intentionally inserted modern cues exist. These cues simultaneously evoke historical distance while paradoxically returning the viewer to the present moment. Through this, I explore the possibility of painting as a medium to “speak the present in the language of the past.” This is not mere revival or imitation; it is a critical recontextualization mediated through the inheritance of form, an attempt to testify to contemporary truths within a visual grammar that transcends time.

The artificial scenes and stage sets in his work act as the backdrop of modern life, space for communication, arguing that we all are social beings. Park calls the figures in his work strangers. They are the members of society, and individuals, who cannot affiliate with or escape the enormous system. 
Humans and their surroundings in our society appear reversed in his work, which is neither landscape nor figurative photography. Humans appear overwhelmed and eroded by the environments they create for themselves. With his work, Park contemplates our existence from a macroscopic perspective, presenting an intersection of the artificial and humanistic.

bio:
Man Begot Light, and then Flow
Light is attractive for artists.  Since the Impressionists' interest in light reflected images of objects and the world, followed by artists like Man Ray who searched the interiors of objects using light,  artists have closely scrutinized and exposed contemporary man existing in a time that has become nearly ambiguous where distinctions between day and night has become blurred, a hybrid time in cities enveloped by artificial light with the advancement in science and technology.
 
Light is a medium that enables our vision to realize this world, and we can perceive an object with any clarity only when there's light.  Therefore light is inseparable from time and as we perceive the world through time, time is also the object of fascination for artists.
  
Jin Siyon has seriously incorporated LED in his artwork since 2008.  In his work titled Wave, the filmed images of sunrise and sunset over the ocean were simultaneously projected in the format of LED sculpture.  There may have been several reasons for incorporating LED into his work, of which the most important would be the artist's formatting of the ocean to autonomously lit and move.  That is, the three dimensional structure required the use of LED to generate form, light, and motion.  The palpable ocean is not a laminated mirage reflected on our retina, but a touchable and reachable entity that is visualized through artificial lighting.   
 
Investigation of man formed out of light
Firstly, hitherto artistic representations of light as meaning have symbolized man as an entity of light, recorded and edited his movements, and thereby expressing the currents of light movements.  The roots of such an approach can be found in the recent developments in social networks.  Represented foremost by Facebook, social networks have already conquered existing confines of physical space, and people on earth are now connected in real time by new online networks.  Such novel relationship mappings have become a starting point to plot the course for the artist's "˜humane' viewpoints.  Furthermore, the artist has begun to interpret individual beings as "˜light.'  The motions of one individual and the relationships derived from human liaisons, the connections between man and the world are represented as traces of light.  
 
This was realized by such works as the media faÃ§ade artwork using LED from 2010 titled, Sign1, which was further developed in Sign2 and Sign3.  In the Sign1 series, the first examples of visualizing light as a human figure were Sign1_Lotte Department Store Media FaÃ§ade_2010; Sign2_Single channel Video_2010; and Sign3_Seoul Square Media FaÃ§ade_2010.  And the first example of clothing a performer with LED costume and recording his movements started with Sign2 and Sign3.  He then moved on to present traces of his data.  The motions of the performer are expressed through movement and traces of light to create meaningful "relationships."  What's interesting is that the artist appropriated a dance format to represent human motion.  The artist uses dance which is motions of one individual as well as the body language used to communicate with the world, and an art of instinctive motions to record the motions of light in an attempt to analyze human existence.  Thereby Jin Siyon uses the most natural and beautiful of human movement in expressing motion and traces of light to represent modes of connecting between man and his world.  
 
Synthesis of Artificial and natural light
Another interesting aspect is the research into visual effects of light which the artist explores by synthesizing LED as artificial light and mother-of-pearl as natural light.  The application of mother-of-pearl as a medium to experiment with visual effects may seem problematic considering the contextual complexity of mother-of-pearl; prone to oversimplification for its sensual visual effect and its connotations as a tradition-bound medium.  But as the artist has continued to work with exploring the natural in technology, his choice of mother-of-pearl fits into place.  Can the vivid and glaring artificial light harmonize well with mother-of-pearl's natural light, or will it be totally outdone by artificial light?  All these doubts have been answered by the form and shapes created by light, and the harmony and balance reached by arrangement.  The dimensions of the monitor frame crafted out of mother-of-pearl have been adjusted to eye level, and the light projection is channeled above the frame.  Harmony is reached by safeguarding the shapes and visual effects of each.

bio:
To borrow words of Fritz Riemann, German psychologist, I receive an impression that anxiety has dual aspects, when observing “anxiety without anxiety”. Anxiety makes us active, and paralyzed in a sense. Anxiety is always a sign and a warning signal, but simultaneously has the character of a sort of suggestion, that is, the strength to overcome it. (Grundformen der Angst  by Fritz Riemann.) As he says, anxiety has negative and positive aspects simultaneously. He claims that our effort to escape from a situation can be the possibility of oneself and the society we belong to. 

I try to show my cautiousness to survive in a disquieting reality and my effort to adapt myself to a surrounding environment through unfamiliar scenes and abstract things set intentionally. This is like a way to survive in a harsh environment as creatures learn how to disguise themselves for their survival. Diverse instable elements in life are like the role of fitting everyday fragments - trivial yet not to be taken lightly - into their right places. I endeavor to excavate and collect such images that remain like fossils between layers of time.

bio:
Blue, the main color of this series, symbolizes the false of beauty that conceals its anxious state as well as the irony of the coexistence of splendor and anxiety.

“Thus every writer’s motto reads: mad I cannot be, sane I do not deign to be, neurotic I am. The text you write must prove to me that it desires me. This proof exists: it is writing.”
― Roland Barthes, The Pleasure of the Text

The proof to Roland Barthes was writing. To me, what proves to me that art desires me is my visual creation, which is the act of changing all the social and cultural anxieties that lurk around me into part of my identity, and my strong affection that offsets them.

MoMo Kim is an artist who was born and raised in Seoul, South Korea. She was educated in New York City and currently resides in Nha Trang, Vietnam.

In her art world, MoMo breaks boundaries between Decorative art and Modernism in contemporary art. Often, MoMo's art is like an autobiography that portrays personal perspectives on the world we are now living in. Through works using various visual media, she aims to share the many facets of her everyday life.

The main patterns of our daily life are created and reproduced by combining pieces of the endless images that are readily available through the smartphone in our hands. Other than these creative activities, MoMo writes about her daily thoughts or create installations that reflect her life. Whenever she feels lonely, MoMo creates abstract or collage works using her favorite images.

bio:
Chang Soon Up is retired professor of Department of Art Education, College of Education, Han Nam University.

His world of art gives out the breath of tradition in well composed picture space.
Outwardly, his painting take on the beauty of well organized composition.
However, it seems that the essence of his paintings is in the world of mentality held in its outward forms.
In such a inner world, he reinterprets tradition and locality into nowadays sentiment.

His process of creation has a sequence of coating of paints with a brush and a roller-observation-shaping-drawing,
covering colours over colours, and erazing. This process of creation can be arranged by logic of casualness on the basis of
unplanned construction of a canvas and expression. Therefore, formative logic of casualness means the relative autonomy of works
discovered by an artist through an endless conversation with an object of a canvas, not a limited form which is necessary autonomy 
construction of a canvas.

His work is regulated as another special quality, that is, unity in construction of a canvas and contents. Formative logic of unity
can be found in the form that an individual brush and a stroke is placed in a right situation syntactically.
Lines and colours formed in construction of a canvas and as adequate arrangement of a canvas make various styles of painting in harmony with
varieties of martiere. Unity in his canvas appears in such objects of boldly omitted and transformed figures and natual objects in contents.
Formative logic of unity is arranged by the style in which faces, hands, flowers or birds are expressed without external descriptions of them
and there are seen ritual vessels of popular Korean religions.

bio:

His practice begins with everyday life and gradually extends toward elements of the natural world. Rather than merely capturing landscapes, he collects fragments of nature to construct narratives about the environments that surround us. His work captures the interactive relationship between humans and nature, translating these interactions into visual landscapes. Currently, he is engaged in a body of work that explores the human being as a mediator between the microscopic and the macroscopic realms.

bio:
Yesang Lee is a South Korea-based artist who explores the connection between energy and consciousness. Her work is shaped by a diverse background in economics, music, and fashion design, which brings a structured yet rhythmic perspective to her art.

Currently, her practice is rooted in the symbols of Korean Minhwa—traditionally used to embody wishes for health and harmony. For Lee, however, these traditional forms are not a fixed style but a starting point. She uses Minhwa as a visual language to study the flow of inner consciousness, currently moving from these classical roots toward a more liberated, contemporary expression.

Specializing in contemporary reinterpretations of Korean Minhwa, Lee explores the essence of "reality-creation" through professional-grade oriental watercolors and natural calcite. Her work transcends traditional boundaries, capturing the invisible light of the self with sophisticated technique.

With a proven track record of three solo exhibitions and multiple national art awards, Yesang Lee offers collectors a profound visual dialogue between ancient heritage and modern consciousness.

bio:
Exploring the primordial essence and silent power of life through a philosophy that celebrates imperfection: "Every line, even the uneven ones, has its own unique charm." The work focuses on stripping away the unnecessary to reveal the raw, organic vitality found in natural forms.

Seeking a tactile honesty, the process uniquely utilizes the reverse (uncoated) side of the canvas. This intentional choice highlights the coarse, natural texture of the fabric, bridging the gap between digital precision and the warmth of physical materials. Based in the dynamic landscape of Seoul, this practice is a continuous journey to capture the still yet powerful energy found in the most honest and 'uneven' lines of existence.

bio:
Born in Korea in 1960, Korean-Canadian abstract painter. I am so blessed  by God, in veiw of the fact that I could have started painting at the age of 40. 
In earlier life of 20s, I had worked for news paper agency for about 8 years. 
Since then, I had been weaving through the occupations like a copy writer, assistant director in  theater company.
Even when I was nearing 40 yrs, I did not realize that I am destined to be a painter.
Of course, I am not a genius like Gauguin, I knew, but I could not resist my fateful gravity towards being an artist.
"It never be too late", God seems to whisper to me.
Of course, I feared skepticism of my artistic dream, intellectual vanity.
However I pondered over the reason why the notion of a painter had come to my mind even belatedly.
That is new vision left behind to me, grace by God, I believed.
I entered into Alberta college of art, Canada, in 1998,
having majored in painting, then finished it in 2003.
I have been working on abstract painting for 15 years,
particularly centering on color field and Minimalism recently.  
I have a strong aspiration of resurrecting Minimalism again since 1960s. It might be reckless challenge,
but also I feel that this too is fate for me to pursue Minimalism now.
On the strength the this style in my works, I offer dialogue with the spiritual calmness and meditation.
Ultimately the fundamental and purest manifestation of my works idioms point to evoking the art of contemplation and the objects of inward-directed quietness in our troubling time.

bio: I divide freedom into three stages: Infinite Freedom, Limited Freedom, and Related Freedom. And these three stages are closely connected with each other and have a vertical relationship. The meaning of freedom changes according to the stage of maturity and becomes an important measure of how people view the world. The meaning of freedom, which began with Infinite Freedom, is constrained by social norms and order and transformed into Limited Freedom. And I believe that this accumulation of constrained experiences and interrelationships gradually progress to the Related Freedom. I visualize the meaning of freedom through the act of confining and connecting the organic forms of nature to the frame.

Lee Woo-jin, known artistically as Simyul, is a prominent South Korean calligrapher and visual artist celebrated for his innovative fusion of traditional calligraphy with contemporary art forms. His work transcends the conventional boundaries of calligraphy, transforming written characters into expressive visual narratives that resonate on both aesthetic and emotional levels.

Lee's artistic approach is characterized by a deep exploration of the essence of letters, treating them not merely as tools for communication but as dynamic visual elements. He often ventures into abstract representations, where the form and flow of characters evoke emotions and stories beyond their literal meanings. This methodology positions his work at the intersection of calligraphy and fine art, offering viewers a multifaceted experience that bridges the gap between textual and visual expression.

bio: After deciding to ‘live a life doing what I like and what I want to do!’, I have been living my life drawing pictures as my job and mission. Living a life drawing pictures has greatly changed my life. I can enjoy the midday sun, and I can spend my daily life much more freely and energetically while seeing the liveliness of the streets, parks, and markets. Also, while teaching pictures, I meet many different people, and my life has become one where I can pack my backpack and go on the road whenever I want. I want to pack my backpack, grab my sketchbook, and go on a journey into nature, culture, and the world, and capture as much of the vast world as I can in pictures. And I want to share them with many people and share them with myself. I hope that through the records and traces of my footsteps as I travel, I can bring new dreams to your hearts.

bio:
Illustrator// 

I first started drawing pictures when I was young, imitating my mother who was a painter. I enjoyed drawing objects around me even before I entered the elementary school, and I astonished people by bold imagination. I kept studying design and painting throughout middle and high school, attending the art institute, and tried to draw pictures different from the exiting frames. 

When in college, I majored in Fine Art, and drew pictures with passion, but my passion drifted into a different direction since I got discharged from military service in 1999. I became more interested in teaching than learning, and I spent 8 years with students at a private art institution. At that time, I taught them design, and my techniques of fine art painting combined with a creative, rational, and design-like way of thinking were well received by students. However, the repeated daily life coupled with the college life I quit halfway through visited me again, making me feel frustrated later on. My life as an illustrator I found as escape out of this routines was a ray of light in the dark tunnel. 

My current job, which requires me to think like children think, see what children see, and stimulate children’s imagination, helped me return to the day when I was a boy who held the brush for the first time, following his mother.I am currently drawing pictures, feeling happier than anybody else.

bio:
Jeeeun Hong is a visual artist, currently based in UK and Korea. Hong works with photography, painting, installation and publication.

Hong contemplates a personal sanctuary; a place where the viewer is invited to discover a personal sanctuary of their own.

In order to explore personal sanctuary, Hong gives attention to the balance between inside and outside to create a space with translucent fabrics; thus, expands the way of thinking through such expression. Fabrics serve as a sort of buffer or protection, being a medium of providing stability between the worlds inside and outside. 

Hong half conceals herself through translucent fabrics, not exposing herself directly, as much as one indirectly experiences the senses of outside by putting on his/her fabrics. It is a projection of her experiences of alleviation and reconciliation that she had when she felt cultural foreignness during the time of living abroad and when she was bewildered between digital and analogue, reinterpreted in her own way and dissolved in her work. 

Hybridization and reconciliation composed of weft threads and warp threads are the process of communication, connecting the outside space with the inner side space and locating the balance between the two. Hong leads the way to take the visual experience beyond the meaning indicated by the form so that the nature of things can be recognized. In this process, 

Hong links her social cultural experience with the balance reminded by the visual mediational experience to go deeper into the reasoning about rest and balance. Hong also wishes that her work can be reinterpreted through the balance point produced from the relationship between spaces of thought that are created through the gaps seen-through, folded, or piled up in interactions with the others, so that it is expanded into their lives and continues on as a journey finding their own space for rest.

Kim Mansu & Rosalie Fabre in Conversation

RF: Rosalie Fabre

Kim: Kim Mansu

RF: Your paintings appear to me like amalgams of vivid memories. It is almost as if you rendered the past alive again, throu your own reinterpretation of art historical references. What importance do your personal as well as national histories play in your
paintings?

KIM: I’'ve lived as an artist for 40 years with so many artistic thoughts and struggles in mind. It’'s been about 25 years since I decided not to pursue paintings derived from Western culture. only about 30 years ago, Korea was still an unrecognized country in the world. During that time (I guess many other artists may have once been concerned with a similar issue), art in Korea or Korean art was a total stranger to people in the international art scene. And that made me consider an artistic path that dug more into traditional values of Korean art while balancing out a sense of contemporary art in the world. That’'s the main reason I quit western oil painting 25 years ago. After I changed my direction toward more traditional methods of landscape painting, I happened to participate in a group exhibition held at the gallery space in Hyundai Department Store, which was a very well-known art space at the time, and realized that even my own people, Koreans, didn’'t even give recognition to our own value. I tried to figure out why and gave lots of thought to finding an easier way to approach the public with my artistic practice without losing Korean traditional value. These thoughts drove me to arrive at Min Hwa (a type of folk painting), which was a long standing art genre in Korea geared more toward a public audience. Now in 2018, Min Hwa is not unfamiliar, but back then it was a strange and unfamiliar type of painting. People hadn’'t been recognizing its existence, although it had always been there for a long time. When thinking about Korean painting, people can easily think only about landscape ink painting, but I wanted to talk about this beautiful colorful traditional painting to people rather than the black and white literati ones.
To foreigners, Korean art would be positioned somewhere between Chinese art and Japanese art. However, Korean art definitely embodies its own aesthetical uniqueness derived from geological and ethnical characteristics. You may then ask what makes Korean’'s aesthetic uniqueness so different from others. I think one good example can speak so much better than a hundred words of explanation. It’'s Korean Moon Jar. It has no artificial intention, but naturalness. It carries acceptance of natural perfection, which embraces natural flaws as part of Nature’s perfection. It’s not because we don’t have a technique to make flawless perfect things, but because we value acceptance to embrace the world as it is. This is a pivotal point of Korean philosophy, and our art pursues the same purpose. This is where I can find Korean aesthetic value.

RF: Can you let me know a little about your childhood and education? Is there an important memory that has forged who you are as an artist?

KIM: My art teacher, who is also my artistic mentor, is Song, Hyesoo (1913-2005). He was part of the first group of people who went to Japan to learn western oil painting in Korea during the Japanese colonial period. All his artworks and other artworks of his contemporaries influenced a lot of my works in my younger days.
In my 20s, which was in the 1970s, I frequently visited the American Center for Korea (ACK), the cultural center of America, to look at art-related materials, such as catalogues and magazines for painting, photography and architecture delivered from abroad. For instance, magazines like Art in America was a very rare resource to gain a knowledge and information on the contemporary art scene happening outside of Korea at the time. bio:
My name is SOYOON CHOI.
I live in South Korea. 
Painting is a kind of unconscious conversation. The Surrealists tried to find creative roots in the unconscious. So, influenced by Freud and Jung's theories, they devoted themselves to creating a new symbolic language that was not there in the past. 
   In this study, I analyzes my work, which expresses surrealistic images based on inherent sensibility. A work of my own is a visual image of the desire inherent in a ritual. This is an expression of desire to expose internal deficiencies and an act to reflect on one's self through conscious consciousness.
   The theme of my works are summarized into two parts : “The Universe as an imaginary and unknown space”, and “A yearning for the Ideal world. I tried to use my inner inspiration to express images in pictures that did not exist in reality. The images of my work reveal surrealistic expressions. The theoretical background of the expression was analyzed based on surrealistic art.
   Surrealistic art is based on unconscious theory. In Chapter I, I looked at the theories of Freud and Jung, both of which are theoretical backgrounds for surrealistic art. In Chapter II, I learned about the time when surrealist art emerged, Max Ernst, Joan Maro, and Salvador Dali. Their representative works also helped me learn more about the techniques of surrealistic art, including Frottages and Automatisme. In Chapter Ⅲ, I named my work ‘Expression of self controlled by consciousness and unexpressed’ and compared it to Freud and Jung's theory. 
   I tried to express a new Utopia in my work by putting the emptiness felt in communication and feelings to get away with it. At this time, the universe was reborn in my consciousness as a space where the desire to escape from reality is expressed, and the space where imagination is realized. Therefore, my work can be called ‘The conscious representation of the unconscious’and it is a subject worth continuing to explore.

Rhee Gyeol’s practice is defined by a radical, self-taught approach, channeling raw introspection into works of intense texture and visual shock. The artist creates a unique visual language by deliberately positioning two opposing forces—the fragility of memory (the rose) against the materiality of decay and trauma (bone, distorted anatomy). Employing thick layers of oil paint applied with a palette knife, Rhee Gyeol sits at the intersection of Expressionistic technique and Surrealist concept, offering a powerful, immediate expression of the contemporary psychological condition through the distortion of the human body.

Dasha Jan is a young artist based in Seoul, South Korea, with over 16 years of experience in painting and visual expression. Originally from Eastern Europe and shaped by a global perspective, her work is rooted in a free-spirited philosophy and deeply inspired by the Impressionists.

Her signature style blends soft pastel tones with vibrant, emotional brushstrokes- often celebrating the wild poetry of flowers, human nature and emotions. Each piece becomes a meditation on movement, memory, and inner bloom.

At just 23, Dasha brings both a fresh perspective and a mature creative voice to her work. Her paintings whisper of gentle resilience and the beauty of becoming—reminding us that blooming is a state of mind.

An artist exploring freedom and transformation through color and form.

bio:
Artist Statement
My work envisions landscapes of sanctuary. The Where Wishes Rest series embodies emotions of recollection, hope, and purification. I perceive earnest wishes (yeomwon) as latent energies—an elemental force that draws moments of healing closer. Through the language of painting, I explore this energy and depict the journey of a heart that rises again.

I coined the term Karmadise, combining Karma (the law of cause and effect) and Paradise (an ideal or peaceful state). Karmadise represents a path toward a harmonious inner state through positive karma and intentional healing. It is a spiritual refuge, guided by compassion (karuna), sympathetic joy (mudita), and equanimity (upekkha), reflecting the Buddhist pursuit of liberation from suffering. This process invites inner reflection, the restoration of emotional energy, and the deepening of the meaning behind one’s wishes.

Within my work, the yearning heart rests in a sanctuary of longing, drifts through waves of purification, and emerges toward light. The repetitive rhythms of flowing lines represent the subtle vibrations of hope arising from inner chaos. I call this space a Ritual Sanctuary—a sacred site that transcends expression and offers emotional liberation and vitality. Art becomes a visual alchemy, transforming wishes into shimmering symbolic landscapes.

My motifs often reference healing symbols: tangled threads act as psychic membranes sewn from childhood wounds, especially memories of my late father. These threads, like a silkworm’s cocoon, preserve memory and spiritual practice. Drawing from Didier Anzieu’s psychic envelope, I explore inner protection as a visual skin.

Canvas functions as both filter and relic—purifying negative energy through layered brushwork and luminescent pigments. With oil paint, neon pigments, and light-reactive materials, my work glows in darkness, revealing ideal dreamscapes such as Wishing Shelters, Guardian Trees, and Lucid Dreams.

To me, art is both light in isolation and life itself—a purified space for the anxious mind. I hope the viewer finds a breath of relief in the healing waves that drift through the mysterious depths of the psyche.

bio:
Hello, I am Guerisae (그리새), a Western-style painter based in South Korea. My given name is Eunjeong Park, but the name "Guerisae" embodies a personal vow I made to myself during my long journey as both an artist and educator — a quiet, persistent reminder: "Keep drawing."
Over time, this phrase became more than a mantra. Transformed into a Korean noun, "Guerisae" has become not only my artist name but a symbol of my lifelong dedication to art and a declaration of my creative identity.

While I spent years running an art academy and sharing the language of art with many students, my hands always yearned for the canvas. Even in the heart of education, I’ve never abandoned the trembling within — the visual impulses that define my artistic voice. The name "Guerisae" serves as a quiet but unwavering promise to continue creating.

I have participated in various exhibitions and projects both in Korea and internationally. Through my work, I seek to weave together the textures of time, fragments of emotion, the rhythms of nature, and the lingering echoes of life. Sometimes through abstract forms, sometimes through lyrical colors and tactile surfaces, I translate my inner world onto the canvas.

My paintings aim not only to please the eye, but to resonate with memory and evoke the emotional remnants of existence. As an artist — and as a human constantly learning and evolving — I aspire to continue a life of creation, engaging with the world through the language of painting.

Thank you.
Guerisae | Eunjeong Park

bio:
Chloe Ji Yoon is a Korean-born artist with a diverse background in theatrical design, costume concept art, and fashion education. After earning her MFA in Theatrical Design in the U.S., she built a career as a film costume concept artist in Hollywood and later taught in the Department of Fashion Industry at a Korean university. Today, she continues to explore visual storytelling through both painting and drawing.
Her works move fluidly between expressive watercolor portraits, observational figure sketches, and richly narrative acrylic paintings. Whether capturing the fleeting emotion of a face in profile or building a layered world around her recurring character “Zoey,” Chloe’s art often reveals a deep interest in gesture, femininity, and inner life.
Drawing remains at the core of her practice. From delicate ink renderings to bold, experimental brushwork, she approaches drawing not just as a preparatory step but as an expressive, finished form. Her style reflects her dual sensitivity to fabric and form—a sensibility shaped by years in costume design and fashion illustration.
Chloe’s work offers a unique perspective where fine art, fashion, and character design meet, always grounded in a painter’s love for texture, color, and mood.
