bio:
Yanghee Chang is an artist known for expressing human existence by combining the characteristics of printmaking with painting. Chang poses questions about human existence through a technique she calls engraving. Based on the idea that human beings are indeterminate and uncertain entities formed by the traces of others, she engraves human figures onto images of nature using a laser on paper. The hollow, seemingly insubstantial figures evoke a sense of existential emptiness and transience. By portraying the human form as an isolated being disconnected from others, Chang also conveys a profound sense of solitude. These figures, composed of traces, suggest that human existence resides somewhere between presence and absence. 
The laser engraving method she employs is adapted from a traditional printmaking technique—typically used to create plates in indirect media—and applied directly to painting. This hybrid technique plays a crucial role in connecting the content and form of her work. As the laser burns through layers of paint applied to paper and lightly scorches the paper’s surface, it leaves behind traces that form the human figure. The resulting image varies depending on multiple factors, including the texture of the paper, the type of paint used, the manner in which the image was painted, its tonal values, and the laser's intensity and speed.

Yanghee Chang, a Korean artist, was born in Seoul in 1976 and has continued to live and work in the city throughout her career. She earned her PhD in Fine Arts from Seoul National University, the most prestigious university in Korea, and has taught drawing, painting, and printmaking at several leading Korean universities. Chang has held 14 solo exhibitions and has received multiple grants from the Korean government in recognition of her work. In 2024, she was awarded the Grand Prize at the Gyeomjae Art Competition, further establishing her as an active and influential figure in the Korean contemporary art scene.

bio:
Artist Seung-Min Oh (born in 1973 in Gyeongju, Gyeongsangbuk-do) graduated from the Department of Western Painting at Daegu Arts University and then earned a Postgraduate Diploma and Master’s degree in Fine Art from the Kent Institute of Art & Design in the UK. 

His recent body of work explores the motif of the city, with a thematic focus on “panic / anxiety” (panic disorder) — addressing questions of existence vs. non-existence, necessity vs. redundancy within urban space. 

His Gyeongju roots combined with international training afford his art a distinctive blend: local identity meets global perspective.

Re-interpreting Urban Spaces
Oh’s works do not simply depict cityscapes — instead, they probe the latent psychological states within them, such as panic or anxiety. In his solo exhibition titled “Just look with your eyes”, he described his theme as “the story of things that exist but feel unnecessary, and things that are necessary yet occasionally unnecessary.” 

Thus, he treats the city as a living organism and explores how hidden emotions like loneliness or pressure may be visually manifested within it.

Fusion of Form and Emotion
His artistic vocabulary leverages bold color contrasts, repeated structural patterns, and distorted urban forms so that viewers don’t merely observe a city but feel it. The interplay of formal experimentation and emotional theme invites one to rethink not only the architecture around them but one’s own relation to urban existence.

Intersection of Local Identity & International Perspective
His origin in Gyeongju imparts a sense of rootedness and cultural memory, while his UK-based fine art education delivers a broader, more experimental outlook. The result is a unique artistic edge where local narrative meets contemporary urban sensibility.

관찰자


I am an impulsive person.
There are afterimages that come to me in sudden moments.
I think of them as my unconscious energy.
Or maybe they are signals from my right brain.

I try to bring these afterimages into conscious action right away.
I express my unconscious energy on a small canvas.
To overcome the signals from my right brain and the resistance of the unconscious,
sometimes, I squeeze paint onto the canvas without even applying gesso.

There are times when I feel an uncontrollable urge —
an urge to act of painting,
or to turn something into an image —
and that urge pours out as an instant emotion.
When that happens, whether it's my left hand or right hand,
I squeeze out more paint and draw out my unconscious with whatever tool I can.

After finishing a piece,
I look at my painting for a long time,
as it stands in the realm of consciousness.
I keep looking.
Even while living my daily life,
even while working to sustain my art,
I look at it again and again.

And then I contemplate deeply and observe.
“Why did I paint that?”
And again, I struggle.

I want to walk this journey with all of you.
“What kind of energy do I feel from this painting?”
“What does this painting mean to me?”
Or simply,
“Why was I drawn to this painting?”

Painting begins with observation,
and ends with observation.
I want to think, observe,
and communicate unconsciously within consciousness, together with you.

Please see it as a constantly changing landscape.
Please see it as something that will not last forever.

Just remember ME.

From. ME

I express the different facets of society through the medium I am most familiar with—crayons (oil pastels). While crayons often evoke the innocence of childhood, I use this blunt and rough material to convey, at times, sharp satire, and at other times, raw and unvarnished messages.

My work revolves around personification, satire, and humor. I anthropomorphize familiar everyday objects to address social issues through painting. Through this process, I seek to create images that fluidly cross the boundary between reality and imagination.

bio:
hello, I'm illustrator from South Korea.
any comment would be appreciated.

My artwork can be referred to as deconstruction and combination of the previous shape or image: an exact challenge to the stereotyped and fixed conceptions.

What is art? In which way should today's contemporary art be?
From this kind of question, my work started and the deconstructive method I have delved deeply is my journey toward the answer.

Art has maintained its life power through people's history, breathing its breath with people. Despite being within the materialized society, art must exist in human life.

My artwork existing in artistic category is asking you what the conventionally conceptualized beauty is. 
Can it be said that the ostensible beauty in our belief is really beauty in itself?

Here are some shattered and deconstructed shapes like body fragments recombined in bright and lovable colors. 

Are they beautiful? Can you say they are lovely? 
I also want to ask contemporary art what beauty is.
This kind of question has led my artwork so far and will be with me into the future.

Art for me is the question asked us thoroughly in life. I hope my art working will be this kind of endless questioning.

bio:
Hi, my name is Young CHOI, an artist working in Korea. My artworks are mainly paintings and drawing performances, and I have interested in the concepts of 'seeing' and 'drawing.'

A bout Painting works
I describe a visual phenomenon created by the distance between the left eye and the right eye via two screens as improvised drawings and hyperrealistic expressions. In artworks, it is shown as if eyes catch the moment that a hand grabbing a drawing tool like a pencil or brush is drawing something.

Each artwork is independently created but mostly two paintings complete one set. Each screen shows similar composition and the main theme which can divide artworks into two categories: one focusing on a hand creating a drawing and the other focusing on a created drawing. This is how two screens are added up to one artwork, implying the establishment of their correlation.
I sometimes use a magnifying glass for some parts such as blood vessels of the hand, wrinkles, or the texture of the drawing object in order to draw objects more realistically than it would be in reality itself. In fact, the act of describing the image caught by camera lens more realistically than the actual object can be defined as hyperrealism, but my artworks are different from previous hyperrealistic paintings in that a physiological phenomenon called Binocular parallax is represented by the drawings.

bio: MY WORKS ARE ABOUT A JOURNEY TO FIND MY TRUE SELF.

We often encounter fateful moments of our lives in circunstances that appear neither significant nor extravagant.
A good example is a simple roll of the dice. Do Min's photo-realist oils record the splash as a falling die hits the water. The title of his series, 'Enjoy the Moment’, parallels Horace's wise phrase, Carpe Diem (seize the day). No matter how high or low the stakes are, for one moment in our lives we gamble on the outcome of the roll of a small cube. Through brilliance of colour and a dramatic sense of dynamism Do Min’s works capture the feeling of thrill and tense anticipation of the final result.
Among the numerous perspectives of and metaphors for life, Do Min has used dice extensively in his work to portray the apparent cruelty innate to our fate, perhaps because dice offer the best analogy of the transient and dynamic aspects of our fortune. Fate is not something that must be obeyed in its given form, but rather an opportunity that is subject to change according to the paths we take and the decisions we make. ‘Enjoy the Moment’ suggests that if we are bound to encounter fate in one way or another, we might as well embrace and enjoy it.
Although a simple object, a tossed die dramatizes poignant moments of our lives. While in the air, the die is ruled by mechanisms of chance that cannot possibly be fathomed; when it comes to a rest, the same die affirms the inevitable nature of fate. From this perspective, a roll of dice contains within the action itself a moment of indeterminacy as well as a seed of creation, and the outcome points to an existence chosen by the action of rolling the dice. Do Min wanted to use the rolled dice to emblematize his affirmation of the undetermined and unpredictable life, dramatizing the impulse and excitement of subjecting ourselves to the unknown fate of this world.
Do Min was born in South Korea in 1976 and graduated Chugye University for the arts in 2003. He has held numerous solo exhibitions, including Gana Art, Seoul in 2009 and Gana Contemporary, Seoul in 2011, and has participated in a number of group exhibitions in Korea and Hong Kong.

bio:
Julia Hyeawon Kim mainly focuses on materiality in her work to express in terms of feminine ideas and emotions. She uses various materials that have strong and wild characteristics such as metals, woods and marbles while using soft and weak materials such as fabrics, crank, water and coconut oil at the same moment. The process of her work starts with burning and smoking these materials. She also uses videos projecting onto the sculptures and a canvas to maximise the effects. Through the contrast of materiality, she does want viewers to see females’ strengths on the one hand, and weakness from their disregarded/unwatched lives on the other hand. Ultimately, she aims to expose women’s rights and interests from her work. 


Julia Hyeawon Kim was born in 1985 in Seoul, South Korea. She lives and works in Seoul and London.

bio:
《대한민국, 김재희》Paintings are a means to communicate with the world to me and records of my growth like a diary.
I have been working on the subject of 'What is a human' constantly,and now working on the inner world of human beings with interest.
As the first theme, I wanted to express a craving for 'freedom' which is one of the human instincts and people living a life without vivid energy while adapting to the repressed circumstances that is already familiar with, by overlapping it with the ‘wings of flying bird’.
Unhappiness could result from an economic pressure, a passive attitude to the power, excessive responsibility or an adaptation to an unequal relationship or the social structure. The helplessness may be caused by situations that make people hesitate though they want to fly vividly
I would like to have a hopeful conversation about how beautiful each of them is. Though they look unhappy now with broken wings, I want to depict them in a break for a while to fly again.
By looking at my painting, I hope them to rest calmly for a moment.

W. Y. Park’s works are about visualizing his hope of going back to the past. The past, here, could be one’s childhood or about a periodic time. Every which it is, Park tries to derive and depict the pristine state that is inherited within us through the form of rock paintings. Although somewhat rough, the unsophisticated lines and surfaces of the prehistoric paintings remind us of the drawings of our childhood when our thoughts and wishes were genuine and pure. In the paintings, the texture of the surface which resembles rocks and caves is depicted with various colors and symbols to express pure feelings, thoughts, and euphoria. For him, it is a way to contemplate what is important in our lives; the ‘source of life’. Through the works, Park intends to create new narratives about our current life by looking at it through the perspective of the past. 


W. Y. Park (born in South Korea) studied Painting and Art Education at Wonkwang University and at Kyunghee University in Korea. Park has been working on the ‘Source of Life’ series for years where he borrows the elements of ancient rock paintings using vibrant solid colors to reflect on our complicated society and to talk about what is important in our lives;  happiness, simplicity, and pure feelings. He took part in several solo exhibitions in Korea: W Museum(2019), Q0 Gallery(2016), Kyodong Art Center(2015), IGong Gallery(2013). 
W. Y. Park currently lives and works in South Korea.

bio:
- Biography
I'm Oul(오울, 吳蔚). My first name is UL in alphabet, and family name is Oh in alphabet as official, but I don't like that alphabet H, so I use my name as Oul - this way is right to call myself because Koreans use their name oppositely(that  family name goes to be in the first.), Yes, I was born in Seoul, the Republic of Korea and grew up in this beautiful town. I've seen many cringe-ugliness plus extreme exotic beauty through this city, as well as our lives are complicated by that, also myself's artworks say that. Oul has lived few countries along the United States of America, Hong Kong, Australia, also traveled in many places. Currently I've been settled down in Anyang city as a working place, but still based in Seoul.

- Artist Statement
My motivation and statement derive from a profound belief in continuous improvement, always looking towards brighter tomorrows while navigating through the complexities of today. I've traversed through periods of darkness, finding myself in a present that neither defines happiness nor unhappiness. In both figurative and abstract art, I strive for progress, each piece a step towards transcending the physical realm and delving into my cringe-beautiful world.
Having traveled to eleven countries, I sought to discern the good from the bad, often resorting to street art as a means to escape the surrounding chaos. Art, akin to a potent drug, stitches together the fragments of my soul, offering solace amidst life's turbulence. My existence hinges on positivity, productivity, and efficacy; otherwise, I might as well cease to exist.
Engaging with audiences fuels an exchange of energy, inviting discourse on the nuances of right and wrong. While art may not save lives, it offers respite from the mundanity of sex, politics, and sports. It provides a sanctuary for thoughtlessness and a platform for illumination.
I paint, scream, dance, and revel in chaos, for within the disorder lies a semblance of meaning. Everything is interconnected, yet nothing truly matters—an ethos I channel into my punk-inspired works. The human ability to appreciate and share aesthetics sets us apart, urging me to wield my hands with greater purpose.
Despite my aversion to labor, it serves as a catalyst for action, alongside passion and fantasy. I yearn to create freely, influenced by the blood and sweat of diverse cultures. In this twenty-first century, provocation incites desire, igniting a thirst for more.
I cherish this earth, trusting it to guide me towards new horizons. While rooted in Seoul, the allure of new locales beckons—a testament to the transformative power of exploration.

bio:
Rakeum Rhee’s work unfolds within a conceptual world she calls the Forest of Noon.
It refers to the moment of noon, when the sun reaches its highest point and shadows disappear—a condition in which all beings are placed under the same intensity of light. This forest is not a physical location, but a state where distinctions, hierarchies, and opposing structures lose their authority.

Within this world, creatures that once belonged to different orders—predators, insects, plants, and other forms of life—coexist within a single scene. They are not arranged according to power, scale, or biological hierarchy, nor do they enact narratives of conflict or dominance. Instead, they remain together in a state that is already complete. Nature, in Rhee’s work, is not an object to be observed, but a condition that includes both the artist and the viewer.

Alongside her figurative works, Rhee develops the abstract series GIL, which extends the same worldview into a more condensed visual language. Drawing from traditional symbols of good fortune, she transforms signs and characters into layered forms that are no longer meant to be read, but felt. Through repetition and structure, energy settles into the surface of the painting, creating a quiet sense of stability and presence.

bio: Muri was Born in Seoul, South Korea, and currently lives in Mexico city.

I began my artistic journey with watercolor and spent much of my school years drawing. Although there were periods in my life when I stepped away from creating, art had always remained quietly within me.


In my late fifties, I returned to painting after many years away, inspired by the vibrant colors and symbolic beauty of Minhwa, traditional Korean folk painting. What began as a quiet rediscovery at a small art studio near my home soon led to unexpected recognition, including a provincial-level awards. 

Through my work, I hope to share the lively colors, warmth, and spirit of Minhwa with a wider audience.

bio:
Ki Yeon Seo is a talented South Korean artist who connects with audiences through her solo exhibitions and numerous juried shows. As a female artist, she strives to make a positive impact on the local art community through her distinct creative identity and continuous exhibition activities.

bio:
Joon Hee Lee is an artist who navigates between painting, illustration, and digital animation, reconstructing landscapes as vessels of emotional memory. Working between New York and Seoul, his practice centers on the intersections of city and nature, memory and perception, drawing upon recurring motifs such as horizons, skies, and architectural forms to chart emotional topographies.
In series such as 《Lost Landscape》, 《Seascape》, 《Horizontal Scape》, Lee’s visual language transcends mere representation of nature, becoming a condensation of sensory experience shaped by time and space. His unique trajectory—spanning both commercial design and fine art—imbues his work with visual sophistication, while simultaneously revealing a quiet, introspective sensibility beneath the surface.
Lee’s work poses essential questions about the act of ‘remembering’ and the practice of ‘seeing’. He explores how lyrical sensibility in painting can persist in the context of contemporary visual culture. Rather than simply constructing beauty, Lee continuously experiments with the capacity of painting to hold onto vanishing emotions and the subtle traces of human existence.
education: Joon Hee Lee is a multidisciplinary artist and educator whose work spans visual art, design, illustration, and animation. He is currently a professor in the Department of Visual Communication Design and Head of the Graduate Illustration Program at Kookmin University in Seoul. For over three decades, he has worked between New York and Seoul, shaping a career that bridges creative practice and academia. After earning his MFA from the School of Visual Arts (SVA) and completing a certificate in animation at New York University.

bio:
I work with oil painting techniques rooted in Renaissance and Dutch Golden Age traditions, with particular focus on chiaroscuro and multi-layered glazing. My practice explores how light can emerge gradually from darkness, allowing form to reveal itself through time rather than immediacy.

After more than two decades of technical research and studio experimentation, my work represents a contemporary continuation of classical painting methods that are rarely practiced today. Floral still life serves as a primary subject, not as decoration, but as a means of contemplating stillness, time, and quiet presence.

bio:
I capture nature, documenting its essence through fragments of color.

-
My artistic process unfolds without preliminary sketching. Instead, I proceed by directly filling areas on the paper. The picture plane is thus divided into numerous schematized color fragments, which eventually coalesce into a single, organic natural landscape. This method is more than simple reproduction; it metaphorically represents the symbiotic mechanism of the great natural world, where parts and the whole are intricately intertwined to achieve harmony.

-
The watercolor medium is central to this expression. Our steps in life, whether clumsy or brilliant, can never be erased. Similarly, watercolor layers cannot be simply removed. Instead, these multiple traces accumulate to create depth and ultimately complete the painting. This layered process showcases the elegant strength afforded by the seemingly fragile medium.

bio:
I am Shin Young Inn, a painter who draws infinite inspiration from nature and strives to faithfully express those emotions through a deep connection with the natural world.

My time studying abroad in Australia had a profound impact on my artistic vision. The blue skies, crisp winds, the scent of grass, and the wildflowers blooming there were not merely parts of nature to me, but fragments of life constantly changing and communicating. The vibrant colors I encountered in nature have become an integral part of my creative process, and I work to capture these sensations in my paintings.

Nature is not just a subject to me, but a presence deeply connected to the emotions I experience and express. Its delicate beauty and hidden vitality are the essence of my work and the source of my inspiration.

bio:
Daye Park is a South Korean visual artist currently living and working in Brazil.
Her work explores themes of migration, identity, and belonging, weaving together the colors, symbols, and emotions of two worlds.

Through oil, gouache, and oil pastel in delicate pointillist or impressionistic techniques, she creates landscapes that blend everyday memories with cultural mythology.
Recurring figures such as the girl in hanbok, the tiger and magpie from Korean Hojakdo paintings, the Baiana, and the toucan embody a dialogue between tradition and new life.

Daye’s paintings are gentle yet radiant , visual stories of love, faith, and hope that shine across distance and difference.

bio:
It began many years ago—the moment I felt clay breathe quietly in my hands.
Since then, 27 years have passed, and I have walked this path with only earth, fire, and the sensitivity of my fingertips to guide me.

I have always asked myself what it truly means to be "Korean"—and how that meaning might take new shape in today’s world.
The traditional patterns in my work are not mere decorations; to me, they are memories, prayers, and living heritage.
Lotus blooms, drifting clouds, the rhythmic lines of dancheong—they return in my pieces, reinterpreted, reshaped, and reborn. Through them, I try to breathe new life into the word “tradition.”

For me, ceramics are vessels of time.
A lump of imperfect clay transforms slowly, through fire and hand, into a form that holds something more than its surface suggests. Within it are my memories, fragments of tradition, and quiet emotions—gathered and solidified in silence.
And I hope each piece begins a new story in the eyes and hearts of those who encounter it.

bio: Artist located in South Korea. Inspired by emotions, memories, inner resonance, nature, contemplation, and meditation

People are sometimes captivated by images without knowing why. Certain paintings evoke inexplicable emotions and awaken a desire to possess them. ROZ defines this phenomenon as “attraction” — a pull that she believes is rooted in the cartoon-like characters that surrounded us in childhood.

Focusing on this sense of instinctive allure, ROZ creates paintings that feature human and animal characters, visualized like emotional afterimages. These figures carry a nostalgic yet unresolved energy, forming the emotional core of her practice.

Her signature character, ROZEE, is a fictional being born from the question, “Does the universe really exist?” Living in space and managing its order, Rozee represents a fragmented self — one that reflects the struggles and routines of modern life. Always by her side is Lu, a bunny doll once discarded as space junk on Earth. Through Rozee’s companionship, Lu overcomes isolation and trauma to be reborn as a symbol of resilience and renewal.

ROZ’s work blurs the line between digital and traditional media, visualizing emotional density within narratives that drift between reality and imagination. With delicate and intentional brushwork, she separates and highlights key elements of each character, granting a flat, cartoon-like form a tangible presence. Her characters explore suppressed feelings, identity restoration, and the yearning for connection — not just cute or endearing, but also deeply human.
“What is it that truly attracts you?”

bio:
Hello,

From a young age, I stood out for my exceptional handwriting, which led me to develop an early passion for calligraphy. This passion grew into a professional pursuit as I majored in calligraphy at university, graduating at the top of my class.

As a calligraphy artist, I specialize in creating unique and innovative works in various styles of Korean and Chinese scripts. One of my focuses is to celebrate and share the beauty and significance of Hangeul, the Korean alphabet. The principles of Hangeul's creation, as documented in the 'Hunminjeongeum Haerye'--a UNESCO World Heritage treasure--highlight the excellence and cultural value of Korean writing, and I strive to convey these qualities through my art.

My works, including hand-drawn calligraphy and traditional literati paintings, are crafted with brush and ink, embracing the elegance of Eastern anesthetics and the art of space. Unlike machine-made creations, they reflect the distinct charm and authenticity of human touch.

With over 30 years of dedication to mastering the brush, I now serve as an Invited Artist in the Literati Painting Division of the Korean Fine Arts Grand Exhibition, continuing my journey to elevate and preserve this timeless art form.

bio:
Hyeyoung Cho

Dancheong Artist | South Korea

Hyeyoung Cho is a contemporary artist who specializes in Puzzle-Dancheong — a modern reinterpretation of traditional Korean decorative painting. Drawing from the centuries-old art of dancheong, Cho deconstructs classical motifs into modular compositions that invite reconfiguration and reinterpretation. Her work explores the fluidity of perception, the cycles of life, and the harmony of color and form.

Cho was the award-winning artist at the 1st K-Women Art Contest & Paris Art Fair (2023), hosted by Womennews. She has represented Korea at the Silk Road International Tourism Expo in Xi’an, China (2015), and was an invited artist for the International Congress of Mathematicians in Seoul (2014). Her work has also been featured in major exhibitions such as the Gyeongju World Culture Expo (2011) and the Hanpyeong Gallery Invitational in Gwangju.

Her solo exhibitions include “Falling in Love with Colors” at Gallery is, and “Puzzle-Dancheong” at the Kyung-In Museum of Fine Art, both located in Insa-dong, Seoul.
She currently works out of her studio “Modern Times of Dancheong”.
education:

bio:
Checksy Choi is a contemporary artist who develops Eotieum—a visual and conceptual framework for understanding how relation endures within fracture. Rooted in Korean language and ways of perceiving relational space, her work explores conditions in which tension, distance, and coexistence sustain connection.

Working across layered paintings on Hanji (traditional Korean paper) and large-scale installation, she constructs spatial compositions in which misalignment becomes a structure for breath, continuity, and resilience.

Articulated through her visual language of Checkered Expressionism, her practice emerges from the lived condition of a divided Korea, extending toward a broader inquiry into how relation persists across distance, time, and rupture. Her work translates histories of fracture into material forms that hold fragmentation without resolution—proposing relation as something that continues to form rather than resolve.

She was selected for HUG: 100 Artists to Watch by a jury including curators and specialists from The Museum of Modern Art (MoMA), Christie’s, and Artnet. Her work is featured in a publication held by the Royal Library, Copenhagen. Additional honors include a UNV Certificate of Honor and recognition as a Hug Visionary Artist.

bio:
I am drawing_na-be, an artist exploring the integration of energies.


My work explores the convergence of light and shadow, digital algorithms and human intuition, and spiritual essence and material reality. I seek the point where these contrasting forces meet to become whole.

The name 'drawing_na-be' reflects this journey:
1. drawing: The creative action of manifesting vision.
2. na: The Korean word for "I" (the Self), the bridge of consciousness.
3. be: The state of existing as one's true, envisioned self.

I often use the mandala as a universal language — not as a religious symbol, but as a tool to shatter the frames that confine us and to integrate contrasting energies.

I hope my work serves as a conduit for you to awaken your inner light and embrace a life of creative freedom where the soul is truly liberated.

bio:
My work begins with a deep empathy for things destined to vanish. I am driven by a desire to 'preserve' the ephemeral—the cold yet warm shadows cast on a building, or the lonely presence of a roadside salt box in midsummer. I find these fleeting moments too precious to simply let pass, feeling a profound tenderness for their inevitable disappearance.

This is why I work primarily with oil pastels on paper. The medium allows for a 'tactile intimacy' where my body heat and fingertips directly meet the surface, bypassing the distance of a brush. Just as the old crayons from my childhood once connected my past self to the present, my current strokes serve as a 'tiny thread' that weaves together the viewer's fragmented memories with the moments I have captured. I create under the name 'Yesterday', for it represents the most immediate and vivid layer of memory that shapes our present existence.

bio:
Singing of the brilliant sunshine,

Singing of the whispering breeze,

And calling upon this precious "today"

Is our rightful duty as we embrace life’s many stories.

Yet, at times, the shadows that life confronts

Are so cold and biting

That we cannot simply comfort them away;

We are cast into an abyss of pain where we must swallow our cries,

Gulping them down repeatedly just to endure this single day.

Walking silently

Through the flow of existence,

We tell ourselves that if it rains, the sun will surely shine,

And if winter comes, the natural spring will return once more.

While the providence of our lives is indeed just,

The winter we must withstand for the sake of that spring

Is so piercing and painful.

Turning our eyes once more toward a heaven

That remains silent even when questioned,

We can only pour out our aching silence.

On this journey toward the great "beyond,"

The countless stories we encounter

Are like shards of wind brushing through wild grass.

Yet, our knees—collapsed by that very wind—

Remain stained with wounds and scars,

Wrestling with the time we have endured.

And so,

This poem of wind, written in colors as a song of praise,

Feels so infinitely humble that I cannot bring myself to utter it.

Instead, I fold it back into my heart with modesty,

And meet this huddled "today."

used to watch Animations for a long time when I was little. Right after watching it, I got caught up in the images of the  animation. They were broken up in the darkness and assembled and ended up being completed. â— This is where Joo Chang Man's work began. Even though spectators approach the work, thinking there is nothing, something pops up, giving out a flash. Merely a flat part of his work is akin to cement-wall back then. And the thing showing up is the sculpture from the dream when he used to visualize. Those objects are the dogs which are the most friendly and intimate with people and the most distant thing in the seabed so called black mouth angler â— Black mouth angler is living in the seabed where no sunlight exists. His eyesight has decreased and he is willing to eat up anything. When you cut off his stomach of it, you are able to see undigested human beings, plastic bags and plastics. black mouth angler reserves those stuff as if they have winning trophy from the war. Joo found out the foot prints of a human being from the black mouth angler He even felt our nature has been swallowed little by little. Despite the distance between a human being and black mouth angler, they appear to eat up a human being which ranks in the top for a food chain. It's horrible. Furthermore, they apparently eat up everything in the world. â— One day, some part of that life came true. I used to live with 4 bulldogs. From the outset, they were really adorable. But as time goes by, I found that what dogs want is not what I expected such as a contact. Joo comes to feel pressure, suffer restriction and be conquered. even though bull dogs are not supposed to be visitors, It's more like preposterousness. At the moment, dogs take a look at the nature from the human being( the most close thing) to black mouth angler ( the most distant thing). They look at everything as the nature. â— Nature comes across as the object for a human being. A human being would develop nature as if we are allowed to utilize it. Does the nature exist for us devoting itself? No. it doesn't exist for us. No purpose has been found yet. We misread it since a human being consider ourself the lord of creation. He made us participate in his work presenting this extremely simple fact. Last, I wish the flashed light lasts for a long time.

Born and educated in the Netherlands, Caroline Mars has studied and worked in Japan, Hong Kong and Singapore for almost 15 years.

Drawing on the five elements central to Asian pilosophy - wood, fire, earth, metal and water - she attempts to temper the clutter and stress of modern life with minimalist composition and simple forms, incorporating her Asian studies of Chinese painting and Ikebana into her innovative body of work.

Mathieu St-Pierre is a Canadian artist who focuses on visual artifacts created by various computer programs and from the more traditional analog video signals. The consequence of those imperfections and corrupted files are his landscapes and narrative images (stills). Also, having a film background helps him to compose with emerging medias and explore new possibilities of the digital canvas.
 
The images not only document the fragility of those virtual data, they are often capable of triggering memories and associations from real world life experience. We are consequently faced with electronic malfunctions in the realm of pixels versus the perfect imagery.

bio:
born in 1970 in Seoul. Korea.studied in NY  

As light....flickering.
His main subject is of secluded countrysides, not urban sprawl. It is simply the landscape itself, devoid of people. Perhaps it is aboutartificial traces, like the wooden fence, grave yards, and ruined country towns that have been so greatly degenerated into their environment, they are difficult to distinguish from nature. In his pictures, the trace is not only these artificial structures but also people as a suggestive form of the past, traces and absence. This artist’s work points to absence instead of existence. It suggests that there were men at that moment, in the past. 
                                            Ko Chung-whan (critics):
Extracted from the preface for Keetae Kim's soloshow "Forgotten Garden" in 2008

Scene 1.
On a bright day, under the deep blue sky, sunlights warmly and breezes gust softly. As you go along a little hill, there was a small tree, making its cool shade by a little meadow. The meadow had a brook that canhardly beseen as it winds it’s way through the overgrown grasses. An unfrequented place, a little while away from the village is a good meadow and shade for a picnic. Probably many people have already done this from a long time ago. Perhaps a lovely couple had whispered here long ago, or travelers going a long way, took a break to mop their brow. Then again,afteranother decade, maybe a severely wounded solider ran away from a battle that was ensuing over the hill. He took hard his last breath, missing the home that he had left. They have left here, their sweet whispers, smells of exhausted sweat and breath. The last gesture fades, with eyes getting darker. A long time has passed since then, the traces that they have left, begin to shine, swaying and smooth as if it wants to show their beautiful days. With a gentle breeze, some of them are climbing far, far away into the sky of those days.

Bae Hanki was born in Korea at 1933. 

Since it was a time of Japanese colonial period, he had gone through a miserable life and suffered pain that comes from a small nation. 

Even after the independence of Korea, the following 6.25 Korean War caused him many hardships and hunger.

He cultivated patriotic virtues and intelligence, and he studied Political Diplomacy of law school in Kyungpook University. 

Also, despite his busy days, he was so sincere in his academics that he graduated Korea University graduate school studying Politics. 

His life motto was to have a virtue of patriotism.
education:

He was awarded a Kyeongju City Culture Award for his art in 2011, and he participated in Korea Elderly Artist Invitation Exhibit and Overseas exhibitions in Austria and Germany. 

He worked at Korean Art Culture Exhibition as a recommended and invited artist. 

Bae served as an auditor and Gyeongju’s vice branch manager for Korean Art Association, and for various art competitions he was invited to exhibit and to be part of hanging committee. 

He was an advisor of the Gyeongju branch of the Korean Art Association.

bio:
As the writer calls himself a healing manager artist when introducing himself, he tries to heal our tired minds by lightly purifying the deep goals of everyday life with humor and humor.
Also, rather than drawing well, the artist focuses on pinpointing the points of things and making them come alive.
Perhaps that's why, if you look at the artist's paintings, you can see unique color patterns that are not seen in traditional oil paintings.
Rather than drawing well, the artist's ability is to pinpoint the point of an object and bring it to life. In particular, the point of the artist's life is to see a deep goal inside.
It is intended to give a fresh and soft pleasure away from the dark colors and heavy and rough textures that rely only on the light and dark colors given by conventional oil paintings.
A writer is a person who can't be seen by conventional writers.
He is a writer who aims to heal by expressing the deep goals of everyday life that existing writers do not say with humor and humor lightly and refreshingly. Maybe that's why when I introduce myself, I introduce myself as a healing manager artist after my name.
